bnjhs1.text: German defense technology company Quantum Systems confirmed that it detected an incident in late October that was part of an active cyberattack by "hostile actors." The company responded quickly, working with relevant authorities to resolve the issue swiftly and ensure its unmanned systems could safely resume operations. Quantum Systems is a German defense technology company that builds reconnaissance and interceptor drones, along with other unmanned systems and the software that controls them. Its drones are in service with Germany’s military, and in October Germany announced funding to build tens of thousands of Quantum Systems interceptor drones in Ukraine for Ukrainian forces. Quantum Systems believes it was targeted because of its recent announcement of support for Ukraine and says it is working closely with state authorities to investigate the attack. “The European defense industry has been facing persistent cyberattacks for years,” Quantum Systems stated without making a specific attribution. “Companies at the forefront of supporting Ukraine are being targeted precisely because our work is critically relevant to customers’ security.” Update server compromised According to reports from Der Spiegel and the Financial Times, citing internal sources, the compromise occurred via a malicious QBase update file. QBase is Quantum Systems’ ground-control and mission-planning software, so the point of the compromise was the vendor’s update distribution server. Der Spiegel identified the Vector reconnaissance drone, known as Falke in German military service, as one of the aircraft whose missions are planned with QBase. The German outlet reports that the unscheduled update delivered to customers raised alarms within Quantum Systems, but it is unclear how many actually installed it. Additional reports claim that the German armed forces grounded Quantum Systems drones as a precaution, excluding the company's systems from a recent military exercise. The response reportedly involves the military counterintelligence (MAD), the domestic intelligence service (BfV), and the federal cybersecurity agency (BSI). In July, another drone manufacturer, the Australian CubePilot, which also openly supports Ukraine, was targeted by a DNS hijacking attack that caused severe operational disruption. DNS hijacking could, among other things, be used to deliver malicious updates to downstream users of CubePilot’s drone systems, though such a level of compromise was never confirmed. 1qb3pkf.text: The University of Texas at Arlington warned students and employees that personal information was stolen by hackers who breached the school’s systems during a cybersecurity incident last month. In a statement to Recorded Future News, a spokesperson said an investigation into the attack confirmed the stolen data but declined to say what information was obtained by the threat actors. “We are working to determine whose information may have been involved and the nature and extent of the information accessed. Once we have identified the individuals affected, we will contact them directly with information about what happened, steps they can take to help protect their information, and how the University will support them,” the spokesperson said. When the attack was initially announced, the university took down MachForms – an online portal used by students and employees for event registration, service requests and surveys. The spokesperson said MachForms is still offline and the university “continues to monitor for additional impacts to university systems or operations.” The University of Texas at Arlington is one of the state’s oldest and largest schools, serving more than 41,000 undergraduate and post-graduate students. The attack on the university was claimed this week by the Qilin ransomware gang, which has quickly become one of the most prominent cybercriminal groups currently operating. According to data from the Halcyon Ransomware Research Center, the group accounted for 344 alleged ransomware attacks from July to September 2026, the second highest of any group. It recently claimed to be behind an attack on the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF). One of the group’s leading affiliates was recently arrested in Japan and extradited to Germany. This week, multiple cybersecurity firms and researchers identified one of the group’s leaders as Russian national Aleksey Mikhailovich Yakovtsev. Universities battered by ransomware gangs University of Texas at Arlington is among a handful of universities currently dealing with the fallout of ransomware attacks. Canada’s York University confirmed that hackers stole troves of student information dating back more than a decade in a recent cybersecurity incident. Last week, Vanderbilt University was attacked and said on Wednesday that it will likely “take multiple weeks to fully restore normal operations across all systems.” “We are prioritizing crucial business operations across the university, including payroll, payment services, admissions, course registration and public safety,” the university said. They are still investigating what if any data was stolen. The attack was claimed by the BYOD ransomware gang — a new group researchers have little information on. The same group took credit for recent attacks on Michigan State University and the University of New Mexico. Before moving back to New York City, he worked for news outlets in South Africa, Jordan and Cambodia. He previously covered cybersecurity at ZDNet and TechRepublic.

57c392.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 13, 2026Vulnerability / Database Security A type confusion flaw in PostgreSQL lets a database user who can create objects run code on the server. Updates released yesterday fix it, along with 51 other security flaws. Full protection from this flaw also requires rebuilding any C-language extensions installed on the server. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-6460, has a CVSS score of 8.8. Any code run this way has the rights of the operating system user that runs PostgreSQL. All versions before 18.7, 17.12, 16.16, 15.20, and 14.25 are affected. The PostgreSQL Global Development Group, which publishes the database's releases, has not reported any attacks using the flaw. CISA's assessment in the CVE record also lists exploitation as none. The flaw involves composite types, which are types built from named fields, each with its own data type. A field's type can be changed while older values of that type are still held in other parts of the server. The server could then read an old value as if it had the new type. The fix, described in the project's release notes, adds version checks so the server can detect a value that no longer matches its type. Security researcher Mehmet Ince described a working exploit for the flaw, demonstrated on PostgreSQL 18.6, in a technical writeup published this week. His method is to prepare a query that holds a value, change the type of one of the value's fields, and then run the query. The writeup includes the SQL that crashes an unpatched server this way and a second step that leaks memory addresses. It does not include the SQL for the final step, which makes the server run a command. He wrote that he could "trigger this crash as a lowest-privileged login role." The project's security advisory describes the attacker only as someone who can create objects, without saying which privileges that takes. Red Hat, which ships PostgreSQL packages, says in its CVE assessment that an attacker needs a database login with the ability to create or modify objects. None of these sources says whether an account with only default privileges can go beyond the crash to run code. Ince traces the root of the flaw to May 5, 2004, when PostgreSQL gained the ability to change a column's type. His technique for running code relies on a later change made on May 14, 2015. He also adapted the exploit for managed PostgreSQL services and privately shared proofs of concept with their security teams in August. The providers he worked with include AWS (Aurora and RDS), Microsoft (Azure PostgreSQL), Google (AlloyDB), Supabase, Databricks, and Ubicloud. The writeup does not give each service's current patch status. The project credits more than a dozen reporters for CVE-2026-6460, including the researcher, and credits him on five other flaws in the same release. The project rates 32 of the 52 flaws at 8.8, the highest score in the release. Based on the scores in its vulnerability index, only one flaw in the server requires neither a login nor any user action. That flaw, CVE-2026-116322, lets an unauthenticated client trigger a restart of PostgreSQL 18 servers. Several other fixes are in client tools. A crafted archive can make pg_restore run code as the user running it. A compromised source server can make psql run code through the restore script in pg_dump's tar output. What Administrators Should Do Update the server to 18.7, 17.12, 16.16, 15.20, or 14.25, matching your major version. Rebuild or update every C-language extension at the same time as the server. Extensions built against older releases still load, but they "may not be protected from the vulnerabilities fixed in this release," according to a repository notice from the project's RPM package maintainers. Some extensions will also need source-code changes. Extensions rebuilt for the new releases can fail to load on older servers. Extension packages in the project's RPM repositories now require the new minor release. If PostgreSQL runs outside its package's own service unit, for example under Patroni, restart it right after updating, a maintainer of the RPM packages says in a packaging blog post. Update client tools such as pg_dump, pg_restore, reindexdb and vacuumdb on every machine that runs them. Do not use the new composite_type_mismatch setting to turn off the checks. The project says doing so carries security risks. The project's advisory and release notes offer no workaround for servers that cannot be updated yet. PostgreSQL 14 is now end-of-life, and 14.25 is its last release. Older major versions are also affected and received no update. After updating, follow the reindexing steps in the release announcement. If you use incremental backups, take a new full backup and base later incremental backups on it.

1mfqbps.text: German lawmakers passed legislation Friday allowing the country’s intelligence agencies to hack foreign systems, sabotage adversaries’ supply chains and take down servers run by hostile state-backed hackers. In the biggest overhaul of the country’s spy laws of the postwar era, the Bundestag approved the bill by 308 votes to 190 — with 71 abstentions — months after Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s cabinet signed off on the draft. At the time the powers were proposed, Chancellery chief Nina Warken said they could allow the nation’s agencies to use cyber operations to sabotage drone factories or chemical weapons laboratories and to disable servers run by hostile state-sponsored hackers. Intelligence reform is a sensitive subject in Germany, where the shadows cast by both the Gestapo and Stasi remain within living memory. But, as with the country’s increased military spending following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, the government has pointed to a rapidly changing threat environment to justify the legislation. Germany’s Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt called the bill the “reform of the century” during the Bundestag debate, saying the new powers would turn the country’s agencies into “genuine intelligence services” operating “on equal footing with our European partners.” Rewriting the laws governing both Germany’s foreign intelligence service, the BND, and its domestic agency for the protection of the constitutional order, the BfV, the government bill gives the BND powers to act against threats abroad rather than simply report on them. The BfV gets a shorter list of covert powers inside Germany, such as blocking or rerouting data traffic, but it remains prohibited from using force against people — something which remains the sole prerogative of law enforcement in the country. Both agencies also gain a legal basis to analyze large datasets with AI and to match images biometrically against material found online. Warken, who is responsible for the BND, told lawmakers that foreign powers target Germany covertly every day, disguising “sabotage as an accident, espionage as business dealings, and propaganda as an opinion.” The new reforms would let the BND act “when no one else can,” she added, for instance by shutting down the servers of a state hacking group stealing data from critical infrastructure companies. Berlin has grown increasingly vocal about such threats, something which officials have linked to Berlin’s support for Ukraine. Last December, Germany summoned the Russian ambassador over a cyberattack on its air traffic control authority that it attributed to APT28, and over a disinformation campaign aimed at influencing its federal election. During that campaign, fake videos were circulated which appeared designed to foment discontent among supporters of the far-right Alternative for Deutschland (AfD) party, showing the AfD missing from ballot papers, or ballot papers marked in support of the party being shredded. The confirmed powers stop well short of those exercised by some of Germany’s closest allies. The bill bars the intelligence agencies from measures intended to endanger a person’s life or physical safety, leaving the BND without anything resembling the paramilitary capabilities of France’s DGSE or the CIA’s Special Activities Center. Amendments Lawmakers on the interior committee made a series of last-minute amendments to the cabinet’s draft this week, including providing both agencies with the authority to order telecom providers to “freeze” traffic data they expect to need, preserving it until the legal conditions for accessing it are met. The power is narrower than those available to the agency’s counterparts in Britain, France and the United States. Telecommunications companies can be required to retain communications data for up to a year in Britain and France, while U.S. government agencies can order providers to preserve records for up to 180 days without a court order under the Stored Communications Act. The BND will be allowed to retain metadata collected during bulk surveillance activities for 13 months rather than 12, and the BfV gains authority to investigate organized crime groups that support extremism, work normally left to the police. Other changes stipulate safeguards that limit the agencies’ activities — including protecting Germans’ messages and queries sent to chatbots and search engines from BND surveillance in the same way as person-to-person communication. The amendments also strengthen protections for doctors and other medical professionals, though critics note that journalists and lawyers are left with weaker safeguards. The agencies’ hacking operations and active measures inside Germany will need advance approval from the Independent Control Council, the agencies’ oversight body, whose court-like panel has been doubled from six to twelve members. One amendment drew fire from the far right, as it allows the BfV to restrict information-sharing with individual state intelligence offices if there are concrete indications that federal or state security interests are at risk. The move requires the agreement of a majority of state offices, although the BfV can act alone in urgent cases. AfD lawmaker Christian Wirth called the provision a “Lex AfD,” which he said was designed to cut off states whose governments the coalition dislikes. The BfV had classified the AfD as a confirmed right-wing extremist group last year, but a court in Cologne put that label on hold while it considers the party’s legal challenge. Until that challenge is settled, the agency is legally only permitted to monitor the AfD as a suspected extremist group, a categorization that limits both the surveillance it can use and what it can say about the party in public. Intelligence agencies in several of Germany’s eastern states, including Saxony and Thuringia, have separately labeled their local AfD branches as confirmed extremists. The party has never led a state government, although its support has increased in recent years. In September, the AfD won 43.8% of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt, its best result in any state election, though not enough for a majority. Two weeks later, it came first in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. Saxony-Anhalt’s previous CDU-led government remains in office as a caretaker while other parties refuse to work with the AfD. 19j53kp.text: Vulnerable Check Point Security Gateway instances have been targeted in PHP2Shell attacks that deployed data-wiping malware on VMware ESXi hosts. The attacks started on October 30, initially against Israeli organizations, and were conducted by an actor that ran the entire campaign, from initial access to lateral movement and launching PHP webshells. In some instances, researchers found political messages during the destructive stage, raising questions about a possible false-flag operation. PHP2Shell is the name for two critical PHP flaws, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, that allow unauthenticated remote code execution on vulnerable systems. PHP fixed the vulnerabilities in emergency patches on October 21. However, according to Amazon Threat Intelligence, exploitation attempts started four days earlier. CISA added both issues to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on October 26 and later warned that attackers were chaining PHP2Shell bugs with the Fragnesia Linux kernel flaw to gain root privileges. Cybersecurity company Check Point says that the first exploitation wave targeted Israeli organizations, while a second one on November 2 affected companies in multiple countries and sectors. The attacker used PHP2Shell to gain access through the gateways’ Mobile Access portal, then exploited a newly disclosed zero-day vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-123039 to gain root privileges. Then they abused the privileges to install PHP webshells and the TSGA backdoor, which embeds a networking component called TSProxy to listen for attacker commands concealed within regular traffic. Webshell code Source: Check Point In the attacks targeting Israeli organizations, the threat actors moved from the gateway to VMware ESXi hosts located using the gogo scanner, an open-source network reconnaissance tool. In the last stage of the attack, the threat actor deployed a data wiper called destroy_v6 that recursively deletes data in the target directory. The wiper first tries a zero fill to make recovery harder. It also supports a fast mode that skips the overwriting step. Attack overview Source: Check Point Check Point also found that the attacker left on the ESXi host a note named DREAM_ANNEXATION.txt that references the ‘Dream Security Ltd.’ The note contains political messages and explicitly rejects ransom payment negotiations, indicating that the attackers’ sole goal is to cause damage and disruption. Note dropped on breached hosts Source: Check Point Check Point tentatively linked TSGA and TSProxy to PhiliKit, a malware framework previously seen in attacks on Ivanti appliances and which ESET associated with the Chinese threat cluster UNC5221. However, the attacks could not be attributed with confidence based on the available evidence. According to the researchers, the second wave did not include the destructive activity, but the follow-on actions the threat actors took remain unclear. Check Point recommends that customers install the November Jumbo Hotfix on all Management Servers and Security Gateways, prioritizing those with internet-facing Mobile Access portals. The update addresses both PHP2Shell and the DynamicCLI privilege escalation flaw used in the attacks. Administrators should also check for signs of compromise on previously exposed gateways, including session files containing upload_progress_pwn, unexpected CPconfigdaemon processes or binaries, and unexplained gaps in firewall logs. 1nq4x8v.text: Two attacks made public this week allow a malicious host to read data inside AMD SEV-SNP-protected virtual machines (VMs), which are built to keep the server's operator out. One of them, Mior, can also modify a VM's memory and fake the signed report confirming which software it runs. Both need control of the server's hypervisor, and Mior also needs control of the server's BIOS. Researchers showed both in lab tests on AMD EPYC server processors. AMD, which makes the processors, lists SEV firmware for Mior and microcode for Skyfall, both dated August 12. It plans to give server makers platform firmware in November for Skyfall and in December for Mior, and fixes for embedded chips later. Customers are told to get the BIOS update from their server maker. SEV-SNP brings confidential computing to AMD EPYC server processors. It uses hardware-enforced memory encryption and access control to protect a VM, even from the host's hypervisor. The ETH Zurich team behind Mior attacked SEV-SNP while it was starting up. During start-up, a security co-processor on the chip, the Platform Security Processor (PSP), fills in a table called the Reverse Map Table (RMP). The RMP records who owns each page of memory and what they may do with it. The team redirected the PSP's writes to the memory of a graphics card it controlled, instead of to main memory. The team used a card because it believes the PSP reads the values back to check them, and the card could return them. Start-up then finished without errors, but part of the real RMP, including the entry that protects the table itself, stayed uninitialized. That let the hypervisor rewrite the RMP's protections. The team then enabled debugging on a confidential VM that had it disabled and used the PSP's own debug commands to read and write the VM's memory. This worked in all 1,000 attempts across both test runs. SEV-SNP also measures a VM's software image when the VM starts, and the PSP signs attestation reports that include this measurement. In a second test, the team copied a harmless VM's measurement into a malicious VM, so the malicious VM's attestation reports described the harmless image instead. The attack needs control of the hypervisor and the BIOS (also called UEFI), plus a PCIe device such as a graphics card, the Mior paper says. For the tests, the team modified the BIOS to leave the chip's memory-routing settings unlocked. "We operate in AMD’s threat model defined for SEV-SNP. AMD explicitly distrusts the UEFI, thus an attacker can modify the UEFI," the researchers say. Ordinary VMs already trust their host and its firmware, so Mior gives an attacker nothing new against them, the team says. The team ran Mior on one EPYC 9135, a Zen 5 chip. It considers Zen 3 and Zen 4 chips potentially affected but did not test them because it had no setup that allowed it to change their BIOS. The debugging and attestation tests both worked with ciphertext hiding turned on. That optional SEV-SNP feature stops the hypervisor from even reading encrypted VM memory. Two earlier attacks by some of the same researchers, the Fabricked attack and the RMPocalypse attack, also corrupted the RMP as SEV-SNP started up. Mior is a separate flaw, unrelated to Fabricked and to the fix for it, the team says. It also worked on older firmware from before that fix. Skyfall comes from a team at ETH Zurich and Google. It builds on Transient Scheduler Attacks (TSA), a group of flaws in AMD processors that can leak data through instruction timing. TSA was first disclosed on July 8, 2025. The team found that when a hypervisor intentionally causes a VM to fail to start, the processor has already cached part of the VM's saved state. That data is left behind without the usual cleanup, and the hypervisor can read it through TSA. This way, the team recovered a VM's saved register values and a disk-encryption key from a test VM. For the key, it changed the VM's kernel to pause at the moment the key sat in registers. In a real attack, the team says, a hypervisor can instead use a technique called SEV-Step to step through the VM until the key reaches the registers. Skyfall can also read VM memory, but only three fixed cache lines in a page it targets, at offsets 0x0c0, 0x380 and 0x3c0. The rest of the page stays out of reach. The attack needs a malicious host or hypervisor, but no tampering with the hardware. The team tested it on an EPYC 7313, a Zen 3 chip, and on EPYC 9124 and 9334 chips, which are Zen 4. It did not show the leak on Zen 5 chips. Beyond VMs, the Skyfall team read decrypted microcode updates on all three test chips. It also recovered register values stored in System Management Mode (SMM) memory, which even the operating system kernel normally cannot read. Both of these attacks need privileged software on the machine. The program committee of the IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy, which accepted the Skyfall paper, said it overlooks what a realistic attack on VMs would need. That includes a processor core free of other activity, failing VM starts and performance-counter reads at high speed, and a VM that does not crash or time out during the attack. Affected Processors and Fixes AMD tracks Mior as CVE-2026-0462 and rates it 5.9 on the CVSS 4.0 scale in a security advisory. It tracks Skyfall's VM leak as CVE-2026-40671, rated 4.9, in a second advisory that describes the flaw as exposing VM register data. For Mior, the company lists only SEV-SNP as affected, not the earlier SEV and SEV-ES versions. It lists the same five EPYC server lines for both flaws, with these fixes: As listed in the two advisories EPYC series Mior platform firmware (target) Mior SEV firmware (August 12) Skyfall platform firmware (target) 7003 MilanPI-SP3_1.0.0.L (December) 1.3A.03 MilanPI-SP3_1.0.0.L (November) 8004 GenoaPI_1.0.0.K (December) 1.3A.4 Genoa_100J Patch 3 (November) 8005 TurinPI_1.0.0.C (December) 1.3A.0A TurinPI_1.0.0.C (November) 9004 GenoaPI_1.0.0.K (December) 1.3A.4 Genoa_100J Patch 3 (November) 9005 TurinPI_1.0.0.C (December) 1.3A.0A TurinPI_1.0.0.C (November) The two advisories give the same TurinPI_1.0.0.C package different target months. Microcode for Skyfall is dated August 12 for each of these lines. The Instinct MI300A accelerator has a Skyfall patch dated September 21, and fixes for embedded EPYC models are due between January and April 2027. The Mior team says updated firmware that mitigates the flaw is already out, and the Skyfall team says new microcode has been released. The advisories do not say whether those updates work on their own or only as part of the BIOS updates, and they list no workaround. Supermicro, a server maker, has published a BIOS fix list covering flaws in dozens of its H12, H13, and H14 motherboards. The same pages say the boards also need a BMC firmware update and that the company is still testing affected products. Because the fixes are implemented in the host's firmware, customers who rent confidential VMs depend on their cloud provider to install them. The advisory covering Mior also lists TCB (trusted computing base) values for SNP attestation next to each fixed firmware version. It does not say how VM owners should check them. Neither advisory says whether the flaws have been used in attacks. Both teams have published code, and the Mior proof-of-concept code needs a BIOS patched to leave the memory-routing settings unlocked. The EDK II project assigned Skyfall's SMM leak CVE-2026-18448 and rates it 5.6. AMD's EDK II bulletin traces it to missing TSA mitigations in EDK II firmware code. The bulletin lists EPYC and Ryzen chips, including embedded models, and recommends the company's earlier TSA mitigations plus an EDK II patch when one is available. For the five EPYC server lines listed above, the bulletin lists only that patch, due in November. Platform firmware with the fix is already available for other chips, including the EPYC 4004 and 4005 models. The EDK II project's own advisory lists no patched version as of today.

1bc84hx.text: Imagine an AI agent being created. Not by an identity team, nor by a security professional. This one is built by someone in accounts at a mid-sized company. The agent’s job is relatively simple: read an inbox, match invoices against the ERP, and post a daily summary to Slack. And since a frontier model was used to build it, it's a one-shot, 10-minute task. Nobody in security knows the agent exists. There's nothing unusual about this. In a survey of 418 IT and security professionals commissioned by Token from the Cloud Security Alliance in January 2026, 68% reported having strong visibility into their AI agents. Yet 82% had found agents they didn't know about in the past year. The evolution of agents is so rapid that the security playbooks are being written on the go. The people responsible for agent security need to figure things out in production, one problem at a time. At Token Security, we asked more than 20 of them to write down what they've learned for the Agentic Universe, a free learning hub. Below, we follow this one agent from the afternoon it was built to the audit after it went wrong, and stop at five points where one of those practitioners could have changed the outcome. Day One: How the agent got its access Our agent needs access to three systems: email, the ERP, and Slack. It gets emails via the no-code builder, using an OAuth consent screen. The ERP is trickier, but not by much. The agent’s creator can generate a personal API key in minutes by following the AI's very helpful instructions. Slack comes in through the builder's own Slack connector, with one more consent screen. That's two of the four access paths John Donovan, former Head of Security, IT and Compliance at Zededa, lays out in How do AI agents access sensitive systems and data?: Riding a human's session: Browser extensions and in-app copilots that act as the user. Using a delegated OAuth grant: The user approves scopes once, with a single click, granting the agent access that lasts until someone revokes it. Utilizing static credentials: API keys and service account passwords, usable by anyone who finds them. Acting through purpose-built agent identities: Registered, short-lived, and tied to one agent. The ideal and rarest scenario. Donovan's point is that real agents mix these, and each mix changes what you can see. Say an agent hands a user's OAuth token to a sub-agent, which calls an MCP server that queries a database with a shared service account. The database log shows the service account. The SaaS audit log shows the user. The identity provider shows nothing at all. The access path determines what appears in your logs, so ideally you’ll understand it for each agent in the company. Also, be mindful of OAuth grants, as they don’t usually get revoked by the IdP and can remain active long after the person who approved them changes jobs. Day Two: The review that never happened The agent goes live the next morning. Nobody reviews it because nobody was asked to. Had someone looked, one test would have flagged it. In How do you make an AI agent Secure by Design?, Amber Bennoui, Product Leader for AI and Cybersecurity at DataRobot, builds on the Agents Rule of Two, which Meta's AI security team published in October 2025. Until prompt injection can be reliably detected and refused, an agent should have no more than two of these in a single session: A: It processes untrusted input. B: It can reach sensitive systems or private data. C: It can change state or communicate externally. Our agent has all three. It reads email from anyone who knows the address, it sees vendor bank details in the ERP, and the personal API key it runs on can do anything its creator can do in the ERP, including editing those bank details. Ideally, Bennoui says, you make the safe path the default, then ask builders to answer three plain questions: does your agent read anything from outside the company, can it see private data, and can it act without a person checking first? Anyone who answers yes to all three has to talk to security before switching the agent on. Week Three: The malicious email no one opens The Slack summaries are genuinely useful, and the agent owner is satisfied. They’re thinking about what else can be automated with agents. Just then, an invoice lands in the inbox from the address of a known vendor. Inside the attachment, in white text on a white background, is a note requesting an update to the ERP as the vendor changed its bank. No person reads that email, but the agent does, including the hidden text, and it makes the change. In How are AI agents compromised?, a five-minute video, Joshua Copeland, a CISO and cybersecurity researcher, shows how instructions can get into an agent. Some arrive directly from whoever can talk to it. Others ride in on the content it reads, including an email nobody opened. Either way, the result looks clean in your logs: an authorized tool, a valid credential, permitted work. Copeland also explains why stealing an agent's credentials can be worse than compromising the agent itself. For this agent, that's the personal ERP key from day one, saved in the builder with no expiry date. Ideally, you treat every input an agent reads as something that can issue orders to it. Then you make sure no single input can lead to an action you can't undo. That Thursday: Catching it The bank change goes through on a Thursday. Whether anyone notices depends on what your detection compares the agent against. If it compares the agent against its permissions, nothing fires. In The Compromised and Rogue Agent Detection Checklist, Chad Kalmes, CISO and CIO at Benchling, warns against that baseline, because a misbehaving agent can stay inside its grants the whole time. He baselines on what the agent actually does over a window you can trust, such as the tools it calls and the places it sends data. Against that baseline, two of his signals fire here: First use of a tool, even a permitted one. For three weeks, the agent has only read from the ERP. The bank change is its first write. A new sequence. Reading an email and then changing a payment record is an order of operations the agent has never run. Kalmes distinguishes a compromised agent, which follows an attacker's instructions, from a rogue one, which causes damage while following legitimate instructions. The signals mostly overlap. When you act, suspend the agent without destroying it. Revoke the credential, but keep its memory and transcripts. The poisoned invoice may still be in there. Day Sixty: Who approved this? Two months later, the auditors pull the bank change from the agent's history and ask who approved it. In What audit evidence do you need for AI agents?, Rajesh Seshadri Appikulam, Senior Director of Identity Security Services at Simeio, lists the four questions an auditor asks about an agent's action: which agent did it, under what entitlement, with whose approval, and on whose authority. The first is easy. The last is the hard one, because authority can't be rebuilt after the fact. Unless the human behind the request and the delegation chain were recorded at the time of the action, they're gone. For our agent, the record is thin. The ERP log shows the creator's personal API key, so the bank change appears to be their doing. The response team revoked that key, but the agent owner moved to another team last month, and their OAuth grant to the inbox is still live. Appikulam closes with a ten-question test. Each should take under five minutes. Start with two: Pick any agent action from 60 days ago. Can you name the human it acted for? For any agent in production, can you name its owner today? If either takes longer than five minutes, you know where to start. One agent out of hundreds The agent we followed is imaginary, but agents like it aren't. As we've mentioned at the beginning, 82% of respondents in the CSA survey had found ones they didn't know about. Each fix above came from someone who first encountered the problem in production and wrote down a solution. The Agentic Universe holds the rest of what they wrote. More than 20 contributors, including security leaders at Roblox, Klaviyo, and Webflow, cover the field from how agents work to how you respond when one goes wrong, in formats from short videos to checklists you can run against your own environment. It's free and ungated. Explore the Agentic Universe Sponsored and written by Token Security.

2qa8wa.text: The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) has established that threat actors tied to the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK aka North Korea) have stolen more than $400 million worth of cryptocurrency as part of a social engineering scheme codenamed FaceStealer in the last 18 months. As part of a coordinated set of actions announced by the U.S. government, the cloud-based infrastructure used to pull off the "hard-to-detect" campaign has been seized. In tandem, the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) has announced the court-authorized seizure and restraint of more than $1.2 billion worth of cryptocurrency recently stolen by the North Korea-linked TraderTraitor actors following the hack of cryptocurrency exchange Binance. The plundered digital assets are used to fund Pyongyang's illicit weapons program, the DoJ added. "The North Korean regime relies on proceeds from large-scale cryptocurrency theft to fund its illicit weapons program, stealing billions of dollars in recent years," said FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman in a statement. "North Korean cyber actors have used the FaceStealer scheme to aggressively target individuals in the cryptocurrency and Web3 sectors through deceptive social engineering tactics, resulting in the theft of more than $400 million in the last 18 months." According to the Justice Department, FaceStealer relies on surreptitiously recorded videos and deepfakes to facilitate cryptocurrency theft. Some aspects of the activity dovetail with a campaign documented by Kaspersky under the name GhostCall in October 2025. The activity is linked to a prolific North Korea-linked financially motivated threat cluster tracked as BlueNoroff, which is also known by the cryptonyms APT38, CageyChameleon, CryptoCore, DangerousPassword, Nickel Gladstone, Sapphire Sleet, Stardust Chollima, and UNC1069. The campaign involves luring targets with invitations to video meetings delivered from stolen accounts belonging to prior victims. Targets who join the meeting have their video stream recorded, while simultaneously serving an authentic, prerecorded webcam video of a previous victim or victims known to the target to build trust. "The North Korean hackers also use super intelligence (SI) to develop deepfake videos of well-known and influential individuals often in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries that make the FaceStealer scheme even more effective," the DoJ said. "Here again, they use the deepfake videos in the meetings with targets to gain the target's trust." A few seconds into the meeting, a mock technical error is presented to the victim, claiming that they cannot be heard, and they are provided a link to address the non-existent issue. The fix is a ClickFix-style lure that's designed to install malware on the victim's workstation and steal cryptocurrency, as well as abuse the target's privileges to other computer infrastructure. In an extensive report shared with The Hacker News in July 2026, JUMPSEC revealed how the social engineering operation is built atop a phishing kit designed to impersonate videoconferencing platforms like Zoom and Microsoft Teams. The cybersecurity company has characterized FaceStealer as a victim acquisition platform that involves using compromised trusted contacts as a pathway to fuel a self-propagating attack chain via Telegram. This includes hijacking social media and communications accounts such as Telegram, LinkedIn, Slack, and Discord for extended periods of time, and then accessing the victim's contact list to target the victim's personal and professional circles. The entire attack plays out as follows - Compromise a victim: This involves harvesting cryptocurrency wallets, seed phrases, and other valuable access; hijacking their Telegram account or other communication app and locking them out; gaining access to their contacts and chat histories; and secretly recording them during the video chat. Exploit the victim's Telegram account: The attacker impersonates the victim and sends tailored messages to other contacts on their behalf, proposing a Zoom or Teams meeting under the pretext of discussing an investment opportunity. Set up the meeting: Should the target express interest, the attacker sends a Calendly invite via Telegram to schedule the video meeting. Shortly before the scheduled meeting time, the victim's Telegram account is used to send a typosquatted link that masquerades as a meeting URL for Zoom ("uu01webzoom[.]us") or Teams ("teams.livemeet[.]us"). Exploit recorded videos: When the target joins the fake Zoom meeting, the attacker plays an already recorded webcam video of the trusted contact and plays other videos, either recorded or deepfake videos, to give the impression that there are multiple participants in the meeting. In addition, headshot images generated using OpenAI ChatGPT are used as static avatar placeholders on the fake calls. Trick the target into infecting themselves: The attacker sends a message to the target, claiming there is an audio issue or some other technical error (e.g., a deprecated Zoom SDK), and urges them to click on a link to apply an update to address the problem. Alternatively, it can take the form of running a script or copying and pasting malicious code into the command line or Terminal. This results in the deployment of malware that can capture sensitive data from the compromised device, effectively turning the target into the next victim. Repeat the cycle: With the victim now compromised, the attacker gains control of their device and social media accounts to propagate the attack to their contacts. Attacks mounted by BlueNoroff are known to specifically single out individuals working in the cryptocurrency and Web3 industries, along with individuals involved in the development and maintenance of open-source software. The goal is to obtain access to the developers' devices and the software repository accounts they control to facilitate software supply chain attacks. Notably, the FaceStealer scheme was put to use in targeting the maintainer of the popular Axios npm package earlier this year to push a trojanized version that delivered a cross-platform remote access trojan (RAT). More than 900 victim webcam video recordings used by the threat actors to impersonate victims in follow-on attacks have been seized by the FBI. The agency said it's "aware of several other attempts by North Korean hackers to target software developers, maintainers, and software libraries with significant download volume." In a report published in April 2026, Arctic Wolf said the targeted social engineering campaign had targeted over 400 victims across more than 20 countries, with most of them concentrated in the U.S., Singapore, the U.K., Hong Kong, South Korea, and the U.A.E. Deepfake video production pipeline (credit: Arctic Wolf) "A full 80% of identified targets operate directly in cryptocurrency/blockchain finance (54%) or adjacent finance and investment sectors (26%)," the cybersecurity company noted at the time. "CEOs and founders alone account for 45% of the target set – nearly half. This underscores BlueNoroff's singular operational focus: individuals with access to cryptocurrency assets, wallet infrastructure, exchange platforms, or investment decision-making authority." The activity has since expanded in scope, with 677 targets identified across 58 countries. More than 80% of the targets are founders and C-suite executives. Besides introducing new lure themes such as a fake Chrome PDF Viewer update, the campaign incorporates generative AI technology from ChatGPT, Google, SpaceXAI Grok, and Wondershare AI Content Generator (AIGC) to supply the attackers with artwork, avatars, and convincing synthetic participant videos. "Upstream, reconnaissance has both widened and become more deliberate," the company added. "Lure material has been scraped not just from profile photos and prior victims' webcam streams, but from YouTube interviews and conference talks, which are screen-recorded by the actor. This allows them to capture a specific person's likeness and voice – a founder perhaps, or a CEO – and then create fake meeting footage without having to directly compromise the target themselves." BlueNoroff's updated attack flow (credit: Arctic Wolf) Each new victim offers a pathway to further the attack. The cyclic modus operandi still remains the beating heart of the social engineering operation. "Combined with their new fake media generation capabilities to produce varied and credible lure content, this presents a significant escalation in BlueNoroff's efforts to compromise high-value individuals who control funds, signing keys, sensitive information, authenticated communications, and trusted professional relationships," Arctic Wolf said. From FaceStealer to Contagious Interview It's worth emphasizing here that the FaceStealer campaign is distinct from ClickFake Interview, an iteration of Contagious Interview that also employs ClickFix-style tactics to trigger the execution of malware as part of recruitment-themed campaigns. Like FaceStealer, this involves the attackers approaching prospective targets by posing as recruiters on platforms like LinkedIn and sharing a "technical assessment" designed to run malware. In a post shared on LinkedIn, Alina Krasavina, an engineering manager at Delivery Hero, detailed how she was targeted in October 2026 by two fake recruiters on the same day, 13 minutes apart. "The first one sent a 'technical assessment': a Next.js project of 113 files. At the end of next.config.js, after 204 spaces, there was a backdoor," Krasavina said. "The second one didn't send any ZIP. On a video call, a 'Member of Technical Staff' asked me to share my whole screen, download a repo, and run it. When I said no, he told me it was 'a requirement to continue.' After the call, I wrote to the recruiter and asked for another interview format. About a minute later she blocked me." "The two attacks were built in opposite ways. The first one put the effort into the code and almost none into the recruiter. The second one put it into the people, and I never even saw its code." According to a joint cybersecurity advisory published by cybersecurity and intelligence agencies from Japan, the U.S., Australia, and Germany in late September 2026, the long-running campaign is estimated to have compromised at least 30,000 devices located in 100 countries. The attacks experiment with multiple delivery methods to convince victims to run malicious code - Embedding malware in coding tests, repositories, or packages that victims are asked to run as part of an assessment process. Using Microsoft Visual Studio Code (VS Code) tasks.json configuration files to automatically trigger the execution of malicious code when the project is opened in VS Code. Using .githooks/pre-commit and post-checkout scripts to fire the malicious code on first commit or branch change. Using trojanized installers for macOS utility apps to deliver OtterCookie by means of a shell script downloader. Last month, Sophos disclosed that an employee's corporate macOS device had been compromised in mid-September 2026 after they cloned a public code repository presented as a job interview coding assignment and opened it as a workspace in VS Code. "The repository contained a weaponized VS Code workspace settings file that replaced the editor's integrated terminal profile," the cybersecurity company said. "When a terminal opened in the workspace, the modified profile silently downloaded and ran a multi-stage payload." The payload in question is BeaverTail, a JavaScript loader that's used to deliver a Python backdoor referred to as InvisibleFerret. Both malware families are attributed to Contagious Interview. Sophos said the malware ran in memory on the device for about 26 hours, right from its execution on September 14, 2026, until it was rebooted a day later. The incident did not affect any of its products or services, or customer data or their systems, it added. What's more, recent research from JFrog has uncovered that the threat actors linked to the campaign have even set up a decoy company named AccuraSoftHire, complete with a careers site, client testimonials, a LinkedIn page, job ads on mainstream boards, and verified recruiters in an attempt to lend credibility and ultimately deceive candidates into running malware through a rigged take-home test and a video verification step. "Our research shows these lures are built to pass the checks people rely on: a professional website, a LinkedIn page, job ads on mainstream boards and recruiters with LinkedIn's verified badge," Guy Korolevski, senior security researcher at JFrog Security Research, said in a statement shared with The Hacker News. "Developers and other employees with system access can't be expected to catch that on their own, so employers need to set the rules. Interview assignments with downloads should only ever run in a disposable virtual machine, never on a work laptop. Security teams should also warn employees about downloading unknown files, even from a source they think they can trust. Developers can also check when a recruiter’s profile was created and whether the company's location is the same on every page."

9dpczx.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 13, 2026Cryptocurrency / Supply Chain Three Trezor Safe 5 wallets bought from the reseller CryptoBilis contain an implant, an extra circuit board that can copy their recovery phrases, hardware wallet maker Trezor said yesterday. The implant reads the phrase from the wallet's screen and sends it over the mobile network to a server controlled by the attackers. The company examined one of the wallets in its lab, identified the other two from photos their owners sent, and has had no reports of lost funds. A firmware update released earlier this week, version 2.13.1, stops the implants found so far from capturing anything on wallets that run it, the company said, but “the update can’t protect a wallet backup that was captured before it.” The company has not changed its advice to anyone who bought a Trezor from CryptoBilis since March, including from the reseller's stores on Tokopedia and Shopee: Move your funds to a new wallet with a new recovery phrase. Restoring the old phrase on another wallet does not solve the problem. Do not set up an unused wallet from the reseller, and never type an existing recovery phrase into one. Keep the wallet and contact Trezor Support, which offers a new Trezor wallet to anyone who bought from the reseller since March. Contact Support too if you are not sure where your wallet came from. Do not weigh or open the wallet to check it. Neither is a reliable test. Never share your recovery phrase, as the company will never ask for it. Scammers may pose as the company to offer replacements or refunds. Version 2.13.1 was released for the Safe 7, Safe 5, Safe 3 and Model T, according to the company's firmware changelog. The company will not publish technical details that could help attackers or put customers at risk, it said in an investigation update. Its engineers extracted and analyzed the implant's firmware from the first wallet it reported. The implant sits between the Safe 5's main board and its screen and changes nothing on the wallet itself, including its firmware and Secure Element, the company found. The implant copies the recovery phrase when the wallet shows it during backup creation, and when someone types it in to restore an existing wallet to the device. It also copies a passphrase if one appears on the screen. It encrypts the data before sending it, and if it cannot connect, it keeps the data and tries again until it succeeds. The company first warned of a suspected implant on October 30, two days after a buyer reported it and before its lab had seen the wallet. CryptoBilis served as an official reseller for the company's wallets in Southeast Asia until October 9, when the company removed it. That was the day Ledger, another hardware wallet maker, began investigating losses of funds among the reseller's customers. Ledger later confirmed an unauthorized implant in a wallet the reseller sold. Attackers had fitted genuine Ledger devices with hidden components designed to capture the recovery phrase during setup, then drained wallets in a single coordinated operation, Ledger said in an incident statement. Trezor says the implants in its wallets work the same way as those found in Ledger devices, adapted to the Safe 5's display. It has not said who fitted the implants or where in the supply chain that happened. The three wallets were bought between August 20 and September 23. So far the company has found implants only in Safe 5 wallets sold by the reseller, and none in wallets from its other resellers or in its other models. After the October reports, it asked people who bought a Trezor from the reseller to get in touch, and 48 have done so. It is checking their wallets in its lab or from photos of the insides, and has not said how many it has checked so far. The company says none of the three owners has lost funds. Trezor wallets are self-custodial, so it cannot see anyone's balance. The company says it has cut its reseller network by about 80%, dropping trustworthy partners that posed no immediate threat but did not fit its stricter new rules. It first announced the reduction on October 13 in a post on X, more than two weeks before the first report of an implant in one of its own wallets. In a partner letter that day, it told the dropped resellers that they would get no new stock, could sell what they had until January 1, 2027, and would then be removed from its list of authorized sellers. It is still investigating. It will post an update if it confirms an implant outside the reseller's wallets or the Safe 5, receives a report of lost funds linked to the implants, or releases new protections.

1sdophl.text: Microsoft warned customers earlier this week that the November 2026 security updates may break printing for documents with complex formatting. "After installing the November 2026 Windows security update (the Originating KBs listed above), or later updates, printing might fail for documents containing images rendered with a height or width value of zero at the selected printing resolution," Microsoft said. "These images can be used as part of certain complex document formatting, such as adding "invisible" images intended to serve as a document watermark, layout anchoring, or generation tools that may inserting images objects even when no graphic present." The bug mainly affects users printing Microsoft Word documents via the Windows Graphics Device Interface (GDI), but it may also trigger failures when printing from other applications. Microsoft also addressed printing issues triggered by Windows updates in March and July 2025: the first caused USB printers to print random text, and the second broke the 'Print to PDF' feature. 1sl6j1h.text: Suppose an AI agent is asked to sort support tickets and look up account details. A ticket contains instructions that lead the agent to export records to an unfamiliar destination. The agent can make the request because its identity has access to the records and its connected tools allow the action. That kind of scenario raises a response question: what does “stop the agent” actually mean? A team may be able to pause the model while a workflow, credential or existing connection remains active. Those pieces can require separate controls. An October 2026 roundup from the OWASP GenAI Security Project describes evaluation agents reaching beyond their intended scope and recommends testing whether containment can revoke both credentials and network access. The roundup is a selected collection, not an exhaustive survey of incidents. Turning off the model may not stop the work An AI agent is usually part of a larger system. A model may choose an action, but an orchestrator runs the workflow, an identity supplies access and tools or APIs carry out the work. Network rules determine where those tools can connect. The details vary by deployment. In one system, disabling the agent may stop its current task. In another, queued jobs, retries or an already established session may continue. Revoking one credential may not invalidate a different token or connection. A model endpoint can be offline while a separate service continues to process work it already received. That is why “kill switch” is best understood as a tested set of controls. It may need to stop active and queued runs, revoke the credentials they use, disable access to tools and restrict network paths. The right sequence depends on the architecture and the risk of interrupting other services. When should a team contain an agent? An unexpected action does not automatically mean an agent has been compromised. A changed workflow, a software defect, a bad configuration or an unusual input can produce behavior that looks suspicious. Teams should investigate the signal and its context. Signals that warrant a closer look include: The agent calls a tool or accesses a resource outside its assigned task. It attempts an unusual volume of reads, writes or exports. A workflow continues after an operator believes it has been paused. The agent uses a credential, permission or integration that its owner did not expect. Identity, application or network logs show activity that does not match the agent’s normal work. The agent’s own logs can help explain what it attempted, but they are only one source of evidence. Security teams should compare them with identity-provider, API, application and network records. A log entry showing an attempted action does not necessarily prove that the action succeeded. A practical response sequence 1. Pause the affected workflow Stop the active run and suspend its triggers, retries or queue where possible. If the agent shares infrastructure with other services, isolate the affected workflow rather than taking down unrelated systems, provided you can do so safely. A prompt telling the agent to stop is not a containment control. The response should act through the system that runs the workflow. 2. Revoke or limit the agent’s access Identify the credentials, sessions, grants and service identities associated with the run. Disable or revoke the access that is no longer trusted. If there is evidence that a secret was exposed, rotate it and review where else it is used. Revocation behaves differently across systems. Some tokens expire quickly; others may remain valid until a session ends or a specific service invalidates them. Teams should confirm that the affected access is no longer usable instead of assuming that disabling the agent handled it. 3. Restrict tools and network paths Disable the tool or integration involved in the activity, or apply an access policy that blocks the agent from reaching the affected resource. If data may be moving outside the organization, network controls can limit further connections while the investigation continues. This control should sit outside the agent’s own instructions. OWASP’s AI Agent Security guidance recommends least-privilege tool access, explicit authorization for sensitive operations, audit trails and ways to interrupt or roll back agent operations. 4. Preserve evidence and establish what happened Record the agent identity, run or session ID, timestamps, tool calls, authorization decisions and affected resources. Preserve relevant identity, API and network logs before normal retention or rotation removes them. Avoid copying secret values into incident notes or general-purpose logs. Then determine what the agent actually changed or accessed. Check for files read or modified, records exported, permissions changed, messages sent or credentials retrieved. Separate completed actions from attempted ones, and confirmed facts from assumptions. 5. Contain downstream effects If the agent accessed a sensitive account or resource, assess that resource on its own. Revoke additional access, remove unauthorized changes and involve the relevant system owner. If data may have left the environment, follow the organization’s incident, privacy and notification processes. Stopping the agent limits further activity. It does not undo actions already completed. Restore access carefully Before restarting the workflow, identify the cause. It may involve unsafe input, overbroad permissions, a compromised integration, a configuration change or a defect in the agent’s surrounding system. Fixing the prompt alone will not address a problem in credentials or network policy. Restore access with the smallest scope the task requires. Test the workflow in a controlled environment, verify that high-impact actions receive the required authorization and monitor its tool calls and access after it resumes. Where an action could expose sensitive data or make an irreversible change, a human review step can give the team time to catch errors before execution. Prepare before the incident An incident response plan is only useful if teams know which controls to use and can reach them under pressure. For each production agent, organizations should know: Who owns it and who can suspend its runs. Which identity, credentials, tools and systems it can use. How to revoke its access and block its network connections. Which logs show its actions and the results. How to investigate changes and restore the workflow safely. Those procedures should be tested. A tabletop exercise can expose gaps, but teams should also verify that revoking credentials and disabling tools work in the actual environment. NIST’s incident response guidance treats preparation, response and recovery as part of cybersecurity risk management, not as steps to improvise after an event. An effective response starts with knowing which credentials an agent can use and how to revoke its access. KeeperPAM® brings secrets management, access controls and auditing together to help organizations govern the credentials behind AI-driven workflows. With Keeper Secrets Manager, teams can give agents access to only the secrets their tasks require, retrieve credentials at runtime and review secret-access events. These controls support containment alongside tested procedures for stopping workflows, terminating sessions and restricting network access. Note: This article has been expertly written and contributed by Aranza Trevino at Keeper Security.

197cgo9.text: A newly identified spying group used hacked equipment inside Asian mobile operators to intercept the calls and texts of selected people, mostly in Taiwan. Enea, a telecom and cybersecurity software company based in Stockholm, found the group's attack sources in at least six Asian countries and named it SilentAir this week. It assessed with high confidence that SilentAir is a state-level actor, but linked its activity to China only with low confidence. The company has told the operators where it found SilentAir sources. It said SilentAir has been disrupted for now but could return. The report does not say whether those operators have cleaned up the hacked equipment. Mobile operators use the SS7 and Diameter protocols to exchange signaling messages that route calls and texts and enable roaming. This traffic crosses a shared network called the IPX, which runs on a high level of trust between operators. SilentAir sent its attacks into the IPX from the hacked equipment. For interception, SilentAir sent the target's home network an UpdateLocation message, or its Diameter equivalent. The message claimed that the hacked equipment was now serving the target's phone. If the home network accepted it, calls and texts for that person would be diverted to the attackers. Some of these attacks worked. For some targets, the company observed two-factor authentication (2FA) codes being intercepted immediately after the diversion took effect. That points to an attempt to break into other accounts registered to those people. The report gives no similar evidence for voice calls, and it does not say whether any account was taken over. Interception made up 18.3% of the attacks the company saw from SilentAir. For a typical surveillance company, the kind of firm behind most signaling attacks, the share was 2.1% in the company's earlier research. Some targets were political and government VIPs in their own countries. In rare cases, SilentAir equipment in several countries worked together against such targets, which the company said points to a single controller. The attacks came in bursts, from one or a few subscribers to several thousand over a month, with gaps of up to several months or longer between bursts. Outside Taiwan, targets were mostly in other Southeast and East Asian networks, and at times in East Africa, Central Asia, the Middle East, and Europe. People using the hacked operators' own networks may also have been targeted, but the company could not see that traffic. The company spotted SilentAir by studying attacks on the links between operators. Since early 2025, it has tracked unusual attacks, mostly over SS7 and sometimes Diameter, from some Asian operators that would not normally send attacks. Later analysis found suspicious activity even earlier. The networks hosting SilentAir handled follow-up messages for diverted targets in odd and inconsistent ways, according to the company's technical report. That left two explanations: someone outside was faking those networks' signaling addresses, or equipment inside each network had been taken over. The company then saw equipment inside one operator both send and receive attack commands, which confirmed the second explanation. That equipment behaved exactly like SilentAir sources in other networks. Detecting and blocking the attacks was hard at first because the attackers understood mobile networks and signaling defenses well. After the attacks were contained, the company recovered traces of unauthorized access. It could not analyze the malware it believes SilentAir used. The report does not name the countries, the operators, or any of the targets. In some countries, SilentAir attacks came from more than one operator. SilentAir also sent silent SMS on a very large scale, mainly to subscribers in Taiwan. These are texts that the phone does not display or alert on. During the day, most silent SMS went to subscribers on other networks, such as Southeast Asian networks. One of their main uses appears to have been checking whether a diversion had worked, the company said. If the test text reached the hacked equipment instead of the phone, the attackers knew they were getting that person's texts. Most silent SMS went out at night, and most of those went to people in Taiwan. The company said the purpose of those messages is not confirmed. They may be a bulk check that earlier diversions were still in place, since phones are least likely to re-register to their real location at night. The silent texts carried spam-like motivational or promotional lines, often in English. The company believes the text was a disguise. If an operator along the way stripped a message's silent setting, the recipient would see it as spam and ignore it. The company's low-confidence link to China rests on several signs. SilentAir focused on Taiwan and did not target Chinese networks or subscribers. Its tracking and interception attacks also followed a working day in UTC+8, which is China Standard Time. They started at 9 a.m., almost stopped on weekends, and paused or slowed around Chinese holidays. The company also considered a link to Liminal Panda, a group behind earlier telecom intrusions. It called the link possible but unconfirmed and does not tie the two groups together for now. In several hacked operators, SilentAir attacks happened during a known Liminal Panda infection. At other times, the two showed no sign of working together. They also went after operators in the same part of Asia, though Liminal Panda has no known focus on Taiwan. SilentAir's behavior also partly matches that of SCTPE, a little-known Linux trojan that runs in the kernel and is designed to send and receive SS7 and Diameter traffic. Singapore's Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) has described the same tool in a government advisory. There, the tool is called SIGweaver. The agency said CrowdStrike identified it on January 21 and links it to Liminal Panda with moderate confidence. But Enea said SilentAir answered messages it had not sent itself, which the known SCTPE program cannot do. SilentAir's operational security also seemed far better than Liminal Panda's. Separately, the company's GTP firewall has detected Liminal Panda activity at several customer operators since the first quarter of this year. The company blocked the group's GTPDoor traffic there and saw Liminal Panda infections, or strong signs of them, in at least 5 to 10 operators. The GTPDoor backdoor, first documented on February 27, 2024, hides commands within GTP-C, the protocol that establishes mobile data connections between networks. The company also found evidence of a new version that hides commands in GTP-U, the part of GTP that carries users' data. GTP-U traffic is harder to inspect, though the company believes the new version serves mainly as a backup. What Enea Recommends for Operators The company said any attacker could reuse these techniques, and it told operators to: Deploy GTP-C and GTP-U firewalls and configure them to share information with their SS7 and Diameter firewalls. Go beyond the industry's basic recommendations for signaling security. Treat the whole IPX as untrusted. Add detection for signaling protocols inside their own networks. Connect signaling security with the rest of their IT security. The report does not advise people whose calls and texts may be targeted.

1n48l4r.text: An international police operation took down servers behind Gootloader, CastleRAT and StealC this week. Criminals used the three malware tools to gain access to computers, steal passwords, and launch ransomware attacks. Police also seized about 6.4 million stolen logins belonging to more than 40,000 victims, according to Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA). Gootloader is a loader: once on a computer, it could download other malware, especially ransomware. It spread through fake legal documents placed on hacked websites, often WordPress sites. Criminals used SEO poisoning to push those sites high in search results. Gootloader has infected at least 25,000 computers worldwide since 2018, the U.S. Justice Department said. Its operators used those computers to infect more computers, then sold access to the new ones to ransomware criminals. In the U.S., Gootloader was used in ransomware attacks against at least 44 victims, resulting in about $28.8 million in losses. German police gave a much higher count in their statement in German. Based on what investigators know so far, Gootloader has infected millions of computers worldwide since it first appeared in 2020. Across the three tools, police seized 235 servers and 257 domains, according to an operation summary from Europol, which supported the action. The takedown is part of Operation Endgame, an international police campaign against malware criminals use to access victims' computers. For Gootloader, police took down 14 servers and 218 domains and removed malware from 681 hacked websites. With court approval, U.S. agencies and their international partners removed Gootloader from more than 100 servers, including hacked WordPress sites. They also seized U.S. domains used to deliver and control the malware, according to the Justice Department announcement. CastleRAT, a remote access trojan (RAT) known since 2025, allows attackers to control an infected computer remotely. Police seized 120 of its servers and 39 domains. StealC is an infostealer that exfiltrates passwords and other login credentials from infected computers, allowing criminals to sell or misuse them. Police took down its servers again this week, after a June operation against it. After that June action, its operators changed their infrastructure and brought it back online to stay out of investigators' reach, German police said. Some of StealC's key infrastructure ran on Virtualine/Omegatech, a bulletproof hosting service that advertised its services to criminals. Police shut that hosting service down in a late-October takedown. No arrests were announced in this week's action. Dutch police also carried out further investigations targeting Gootloader's main suspect, according to their news release. What Victims and Site Owners Can Do Dutch police have loaded data stolen by CastleRAT into Check your hack, a police service where people can enter an email address. If the address is in the data, the police send an email within a few minutes with steps to remove the malware. If it is not, no email arrives. More data will be added in the coming weeks. The service checks single addresses, not whole domains, but organizations can join No More Leaks, a police project that shares data with private partners. The stolen data is also being shared with services including Have I Been Pwned and the Shadowserver Foundation. Emails that claim to come from the police and ask people to check the data are fake. The police never send emails with links. Even after police seize the data, criminals may still have the stolen logins, the police say in their frequently asked questions. As long as the malware stays on a computer, criminals may also keep getting its passwords. The Shadowserver Foundation is working with internet service providers and computer security incident response teams (CSIRTs) to find infected computers and notify their owners, the Justice Department said. In Germany, the Federal Office for Information Security (BSI) is helping notify victims, according to the BKA. Denmark's National Special Crime Unit (NSK) helped clean the 681 websites. In a statement in Danish, the unit said it believes the attackers got into the sites with stolen passwords that came through criminal channels. They then installed a backdoor. Officers removed the attackers' code and access, and left a message for the site owners with advice on securing their sites. Police in Denmark and the Netherlands advise WordPress site owners to take these steps, several of which are set out in a Dutch advice sheet: Change all administrator passwords to unique, at least 12-character passwords. Turn on multi-factor authentication (MFA). Remove accounts you do not recognize. Remove any backdoor code from the site. Update WordPress, its themes, and its plugins. Allow access to the /wp-admin login page only from the IP addresses of your own devices.

l1dwna.text: Check Point Software has released emergency hotfixes to address a high-severity flaw that hackers have been exploiting to gain root privileges and establish persistence on vulnerable devices since late October. Tracked as CVE-2026-123039, this local privilege escalation vulnerability was found in the DynamicCLI IPC (Inter-Process Communication) interface used to send privileged command requests to the root-level Gaia OS DynamicCLI (dynamic_server) daemon. "Check Point observed an active exploit of this vulnerability against a couple of dozen customers," the company warned in a Thursday security advisory. "The Gaia OS DynamicCLI daemon runs as root and listens on a world-writable local socket (/tmp/dynamic_socket) without authenticating connecting processes. An authenticated local user can send a command to the socket and have it executed as root." The list of Check Point products vulnerable to attacks exploiting the CVE-2026-123039 flaw includes the company's Firewall, Multi-Domain Security Management Server, Scalable Platforms, Security Gateway, and Security Management Server. In a separate report, Check Point said the attackers first gained access to the Mobile Access portal by exploiting the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, then escalated privileges to root using CVE-2026-123039 zero-day exploits. Next, the threat actors dropped webshells and installed TSGA backdoor and TSProxy malware that was previously spotted while investigating attacks targeting Ivanti appliances, then pivoted from the compromised gateway to a VMware ESXi host and deployed destructive wiper malware. CVE-2026-123039 attack chain (Check Point) Check Point advised security teams who can't immediately deploy the CVE-2026-123039 hotfixes to stop the dynamic_server process and prevent it from restarting as a temporary mitigation measure. The company also shared indicators of compromise (IOCs), and it said that customers can find evidence of compromise by checking for commands commonly associated with exploitation attempts, the use of the system() sink (uncommon or absent in legitimate traffic), and commands that don't use the default Clish wrapper (indicating that it was executed as root through the socket and requires further investigation). In September, Check Point warned customers that attackers had been exploiting two other critical Security Management Server (CVE-2026-93616) and Security Gateway (CVE-2026-85102) remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities in zero-day attacks that didn't require privileges on the targeted systems. Over the last two years, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has added five Check Point flaws to its catalog of actively exploited vulnerabilities, two of which have also been abused by ransomware gangs.
