1ycxb7y.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 10, 2026Vulnerability / Mobile Security An iMessage flaw could let a remote attacker join a group chat and receive its messages, Apple said yesterday, and it released updates to fix it. The updates also fix a separate iMessage flaw that could let someone added to a group access messages sent before they joined. As of today, other updates released yesterday for the iPhone XS, XS Max and XR, the iPad (7th generation) and some Apple Watch models do not list either fix. The company's notes also do not say whether either flaw has been exploited, what an attacker would need, whether group members would see someone who joined this way, or whether every member must update to be protected. The updates that fix the iMessage flaws also fix a flaw in Google's Brotli compression library. The notes do not mention any attacks using that flaw. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 27. The flaw that could let a remote attacker join a group chat is tracked as CVE-2026-113961. It is an authorization issue that the updates fix through improved validation. The flaw involving earlier messages is CVE-2026-113960. Which Updates Carry the Fixes Each operating system version got its own update. The security advisory for iOS and iPadOS 27.2.1 describes all three flaws. The security releases list links to the notes for every update. The iOS 18.7.12 notes and the watchOS 26.6.1 notes list other security fixes but not the iMessage or Brotli fixes. The company does not say whether devices on those versions are affected by the three flaws. Its notes also offer no workaround for anyone who cannot update right away. The Brotli flaw, CVE-2026-111497, is an out-of-bounds write in the library's decoder that could let malicious input corrupt memory. CISA's catalog entry for the Brotli decoder flaw names Google's Brotli as the affected product and says different products could use the component. All nine updates fix Bluetooth and AirPlay flaws. Two could allow a malicious Bluetooth device, or an attacker within Bluetooth range, to pair with a device without user interaction. The notes do not say what a paired device could then do. Two others could let an attacker bypass the limit on pairing code attempts, one from Bluetooth range and one from the same network. Another could let an attacker in Bluetooth range corrupt process memory.

1wdf40n.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 10, 2026Cyber Espionage / Malware The Russia-aligned state-sponsored threat actor known as Turla (aka Snake) is wielding a previously undocumented cyber espionage toolset called Cereal that's used to break into victims' Microsoft Exchange servers with an aim to surreptitiously collect emails. According to an ESET report shared with The Hacker News ahead of publication, the sophisticated and modular tool is designed for long-term intelligence gathering and has been observed against two governmental entities in Kazakhstan and Romania in late 2025. "The Cereal toolset is a carefully constructed instrument for long-term, stealthy cyber espionage," the Slovakian cybersecurity company said. "It leaves little on disk, avoids external infrastructure that could be discovered and blocked, and conceals itself within legitimate Exchange processes." "The Cereal toolset demonstrates that, for Turla, Exchange servers are not just mail servers – they are durable collection points, internal execution hubs, and a suitable environment for hiding sophisticated .NET tradecraft." The toolset is a collection of interconnected components that are capable of running on Microsoft Exchange servers, receiving commands, executing them in memory, mapping the infected network, and harvesting emails of interest. The initial access vector used to deliver the malware is unknown, although the group is known to conduct spear-phishing, watering hole, and ISP-level adversary-in-the-middle (AitM) attacks. Cereal gets its name from the fact that the tools make extensive use of serialization, which refers to the process of converting a data structure or an object's state into a format that can be easily stored, transmitted, and reconstructed. A number of aspects make the malware stand apart - Absence of an external command-and-control (C2) infrastructure, instead abusing a compromised Exchange server for this purpose. Sending commands in the form of separate, compiled .NET programs. Using an automated email collection module, which is injected into legitimate Microsoft Exchange processes and is engineered to manipulate the email transport pipeline. The combination of these techniques shows that the threat actor possesses a deep understanding of the internal workings of Microsoft Exchange, ESET added. The Cereal framework consists of eight moving parts that work together to provide the attackers with access to sensitive email data - CerealRunner, which is deployed by the operator and serves as a pathway for dropping additional components, including CerealLoader, CerealSprinter, CerealIron, and CerealMoth. CerealLoader, which loads and runs a .NET assembly from an encrypted file on disk, leading to the execution of CerealSprinter. CerealSprinter, which functions similarly to CerealRunner and is used to decrypt and run CerealNeuron, CerealHermit, and CerealBox. CerealIron, an injector that makes it possible to load and run .NET assemblies from non .NET processes. CerealMoth, which receives an assembly and a method name as inputs, loads the assembly, and runs the specified method. CerealNeuron, a passive backdoor that runs on a compromised Exchange Server and listens for incoming web requests on paths that appear like regular Exchange traffic to execute assemblies contained in CerealRunner binaries. CerealHermit, a variant of CerealNeuron that reads commands from encrypted files on disk and has no network functionality of its own. CerealBox, which is the email harvesting module that processes, filters, and collects email messages by injecting itself into the Exchange transport service ("EdgeTransport.exe"). Upon gaining visibility into the email flow, the malware looks for messages containing DOC, DOCX, or PDF attachments, and matches at least one of many hard-coded lists with sender addresses, recipient addresses, subject lines, or attachment names. Emails that meet the filtering criteria are compressed, encrypted, and staged in files on disk, after which they are exfiltrated and deleted via CerealNeuron commands. In the attack aimed at the Romanian government organization, CerealBox is said to have been configured to gather emails involving NATO and European Union institutional addresses, a pattern that aligns with Russia's strategic priorities. The commands delivered as compiled .NET programs are handled by CerealRunner, which unpacks and executes the payloads in memory and then sends the results back to CerealNeuron for subsequent exfiltration to the threat actor in encrypted format. The commands support retrieving mailboxes or specific messages; queuing Active Directory for computers, users, groups, and DNS records; running Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) queries; extracting LSA Secrets; listing volume snapshots; and performing file operations. "The sheer volume of near-identical binaries, each compiled for a specific task, strongly suggests that the operators have an internal framework that automates the compilation and packaging of commands," ESET researcher Matías Porolli said. "Combined with a codebase built around modular, interchangeable components, the impression is one of a mature, well-engineered platform – rather than a loose collection of scripts."

keytmj.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 10, 2026Vulnerability / Enterprise Security Four flaws that attackers could exploit without logging in were fixed today as part of SAP's monthly Security Patch Day—the vendor rates all four 10.0, the maximum CVSS score. Three are in the SAP NetWeaver application server, the software SAP systems run on, and one is in the Web Dispatcher, which receives web requests from the internet and passes them on to that server. The flaws in the Web Dispatcher and the Internet Communication Manager (ICM), which handles the server's web traffic, could allow an attacker who can reach the software over the network to run code, the vendor says. The flaw in the server's SAML 2.0 service provider, which hands off user sign-in to an identity provider, could allow an attacker to log in as any user on some systems that use SAML single sign-on. The flaw in SAP Gateway, which connects the server to other SAP systems and programs, could allow an attacker to impersonate one of the system's own servers and take unauthorized actions. None of the four require any user action to work. Affected Versions and SAP Notes Each flaw is fixed in its own note, and the affected versions differ by component, according to SAP's November security bulletin. The notes are in SAP for Me, which requires a sign-in, and the vendor strongly recommends applying them as a priority. CVE Component SAP Note Affected versions CVE-2026-76964 Internet Communication Manager (ICM), SAP NetWeaver AS ABAP Note 3778530 KRNL64UC 7.53, KERNEL 7.53, 7.54, 7.77, 7.93, 9.16, 9.18, 9.20 CVE-2026-89126 SAP Web Dispatcher Note 3778556 HDB 2.00, KRNL64UC 7.53, WEBDISP 7.53, 7.54, 7.77, 7.93, 9.16, XS_ADVANCED_RUNTIME 1.00, SAP_EXTENDED_APP_SERVICES 1, KERNEL 7.53, 7.54, 7.77, 7.93, 9.16, 9.18, 9.20 CVE-2026-89103 SAP Gateway Note 3798345 KRNL64NUC 7.22, 7.22EXT, KRNL64UC 7.22, 7.22EXT, 7.53, 8.04, KERNEL 7.22, 7.53, 7.54, 7.77, 7.93, 8.04, 9.16, 9.20, 9.21 CVE-2026-120017 SAML2 service provider, SAP NetWeaver AS ABAP and ABAP Platform Note 3849308 SAP_BASIS 702, 731, 740, 750, 751, 752, 753, 754, 755, 756, 757, 758, 816, 920, 921, 922 What Each Flaw Allows On the affected SAML setups, an attacker could use CVE-2026-120017 to log in as privileged users too, according to the vendor. A full compromise could follow, possibly reaching connected systems. A different SAML flaw in the same software, CVE-2026-44748, was fixed on June 9 and needed an attacker with a normal user account. In the ICM flaw (CVE-2026-76964) and the Web Dispatcher flaw (CVE-2026-89126), crafted network traffic could corrupt memory. An attacker who succeeds could then run code and fully compromise the system. SAP Gateway uses access control lists to decide which outside programs may connect to it and which programs it may start. In CVE-2026-89103, the gateway enables its default list with high privileges, allowing an external attacker to be treated as one of the system's own application servers. That attacker could then take unauthorized actions in the application environment. What to Do In its Patch Day analysis, RedRays, a company that reviewed the notes in SAP for Me today, advises updating the kernel and all Web Dispatchers in a single rollout. That rollout should reach levels that cover all 17 of this month's kernel and Web Dispatcher fixes. The firm's guidance for each flaw: SAML2 (CVE-2026-120017). Under certain configurations, the service provider did not check signatures on incoming assertions. Treat any AS ABAP system that uses SAML2 for browser logon, such as Fiori Launchpad or Web GUI behind an identity provider, as in scope until shown otherwise. There is no workaround, so the correction instructions or the listed support package are the only fix. The firm's SAML2 analysis also suggests reviewing every trusted identity provider in transaction SAML2 and checking audit logs for SAML logons by privileged users from unexpected sources. SAP Gateway (CVE-2026-89103). Where secinfo and reginfo hold no explicit rules, or rely on the internal host keyword, the gateway falls back to rules that allow the system's own application servers. An attacker who passes as one of them could then reach the usual gateway attack paths toward command execution. The note lists no workaround. For kernels up to 7.77, the fix adds the profile parameter gw/acl_mode_proxy, which tightens the default rules, while kernels from 7.93 on already have it. The firm's Gateway analysis advises setting it after patching and checking that gw/acl_mode is 1, that secinfo and reginfo hold explicit rules, and that the gateway port (33xx) cannot be reached from user networks or the internet. ICM (CVE-2026-76964). WebSocket control frames with invalid length fields cause a heap out-of-bounds write before any login. SAP NetWeaver AS Java is not affected, and the fix ships through dw.sar and the SP Stack Kernel. If users reach the ICM only through a Web Dispatcher, patching that Web Dispatcher to the levels in FAQ note 3778788 shields the ICM for now, according to the firm's ICM analysis. That holds only if nobody can reach the ICM ports directly. Turning off WebSocket support blocks the bug as a last resort, but it breaks features that depend on it. Web Dispatcher (CVE-2026-89126). It has the same root cause as the ICM flaw. It affects standalone and embedded Web Dispatchers, including those in SAP HANA XS Classic and XS Advanced, but not SAP Content Server. The firm's Web Dispatcher analysis lists the patch paths: SAPWEBDISP.SAR for standalone instances, dw.sar or the SP Stack Kernel for embedded ones, SPS08 revision 089.05 or SPS07 revision 079.11 for HANA XS Classic, and version 1.5.4 or later for XS Advanced. Turning off WebSocket support works until the patch is in, but the note warns that this affects ABAP Push Channels and some Fiori features. Find every Web Dispatcher first, because one missed instance leaves the flaw open.

l5yu54.text: An October cyberattack on refrigeration controllers at about 700 French retail sites was carried out by a cyber unit of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), the French government said yesterday. The attackers broke into controllers on the night of October 11 and changed their defrost settings to high temperatures. That caused food losses and, in at least 15 cases, fires. The unit is called Shahid Kaveh. It is known mainly through hacktivist personas, such as CyberAveng3rs and Cyber Isnaad Front, that publicly claim some of its attacks, France says. France's Foreign Ministry plans to summon Iran's ambassador and to ask its European partners to adopt new sanctions against Iranian organizations and individuals involved in the attack. The Paris prosecutor's office opened a judicial investigation yesterday against the unit's head, the head's two deputies and anyone else identified. It has asked for international arrest warrants. The offenses under investigation include illegally interfering with computer systems and causing damage by means dangerous to people, both made more serious by the aim of serving a foreign power, Iran. In the October attack, the attackers took remote control of Danfoss and Dixell refrigeration controllers through web interfaces, the prosecutor's office said in a press release. They started abnormal defrost cycles with no time limit and switched off the temperature probes' safety alerts, which should go off above a certain temperature. The attack caused about 20 fires. Most of the organizations hit were large retailers, according to a joint report by France's cyber crisis coordination center, known as C4. They include Casino, Leclerc, Coopérative U, Metro, Carrefour and Intermarché. Small butcher shops, a slaughterhouse and cooperative food plants were also among the victims. The center also tied the attack to the simultaneous targeting of Schneider Electric equipment at several small hydroelectric installations in France. The effects on that equipment were moderate. In its attribution statement, the ministry estimated the food losses at several tens of millions of euros and called the operation the first offensive cyber campaign on French soil carried out purely for sabotage. How France Tied the Attack to Iran The C4 brings together France's national cybersecurity agency (ANSSI), the DGSE and DGSI security services, the armament directorate and the cyber defense command. It says four indicators point to the IRGC as the sponsor of the attack and to Shahid Kaveh as the unit that carried it out. The infrastructure used in the attack was also used during the same period for reconnaissance of Schneider Electric equipment. That equipment is installed at sites such as small- and medium-sized energy and water production sites. The reconnaissance relied on techniques that Shahid Kaveh has used since at least April. The attackers also used FOFA, a scanning tool they usually use. CyberbanNews, a propaganda outlet linked to the unit, reported on the attack as early as October 13. The attack infrastructure also held traces of Persian. Prosecutors said the criminal investigation, run by France's anti-cybercrime office (OFAC) and the DGSI, found an attack method typical of the unit. It also found the use of Persian and IP addresses leading to devices located in Iran. Shahid Kaveh has previously claimed attacks on industrial equipment, according to C4. Through CyberAveng3rs, it claimed an earlier campaign against Unitronics, an Israeli company that makes industrial control systems, in November 2023. In March and April, it claimed a large sabotage campaign against Israeli and U.S. interests that hit industrial control equipment, including Israeli refrigeration equipment. France's attribution does not mention the new wave of refrigeration attacks that struck supermarkets in several other European countries last week. What Operators Should Do France's CERT-FR said in an incident alert that it was aware of numerous compromises affecting remote refrigeration controllers across four product families. They are the Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC series, the Copeland xweb, and the Dixell xweb. The alert, last updated on October 16, warned that attack campaigns against this equipment were probably still underway, and that exposing a management interface to the internet goes against good practice. For controllers that are not compromised, the alert's steps are: Remove internet exposure from these units and from any unit reachable at a public IP address. Check insurance contract terms before cutting off the data feed to the refrigeration contractor. Review the full configuration, especially the defrost ranges. Restore access only through a secure VPN or a protected network. In an emergency, filtering the contractors' IP addresses at a firewall is possible, but it is not a lasting fix. Follow the maker's recommended practices. For Danfoss devices, this includes updating firmware, setting the security level to Strict, and ensuring default passwords have been changed. For compromised controllers, the steps are: Remove internet exposure and check insurance terms, as above. Restart Danfoss equipment, or otherwise restore the device to its factory settings. Restore access only through a secure VPN or a protected network. As above, firewall filtering of contractors' IP addresses is an emergency option, not a lasting fix. Reconfigure the device before putting it back into service, then follow the maker's recommended practices. An end-of-life (EOL) device that receives no security fixes faces a very high risk of compromise if it remains exposed to the internet, the alert warns. In that case, a factory reset alone is not enough: it removes the attackers' persistence, but the device stays vulnerable and will almost certainly be compromised again.

1fa3i4t.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 10, 2026Artificial Intelligence / Application Security Anthropic on Monday released Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 models, which it said exhibit improvements in coding, reasoning, and vision. "On CyScenarioBench, GPT-6 Cyber completed 11 of 11 long-horizon scenarios at least once, compared with 8 of 11 for GPT-6 Astra. Average success rates were 97% in vulnerability research and exploitation, 98% in network attack simulation, and 63% in evasion." Fable 5.2 also scored 89.6% on the CVE Rediscovery benchmark, Anthropic's own internal evaluation of whether an AI model can independently rediscover known vulnerabilities given only the affected source code. The assessment includes 1,829 advisories for open-source projects published in October 2026. Claude Fable 5.2 is available on all platforms, including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. oj5ea3.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 10, 2026Vulnerability / Browser Security Google on Monday released updates to patch nine security vulnerabilities, including one that has come under active exploitation in the wild. The high-severity vulnerability, assigned the CVE identifier CVE-2026-125350 (CVSS score: N/A), has been described as a use-after-free bug in the XML component. Use-after-free bugs typically occur when a program attempts to access a memory location after it has already been freed. Successful exploitation of these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to achieve data corruption, program crashes, or arbitrary code execution. An anonymous security researcher has been credited with discovering and reporting the flaw on November 6, 2026. Google acknowledged it is "aware that an exploit for CVE-2026-125350 exists in the wild," but has not revealed any additional specific information related to how it's being abused in real-world attacks or who is behind them. "Access to bug details and links may be kept restricted until a majority of users are updated with a fix," the tech giant added. "We will also retain restrictions if the bug exists in a third-party library that other projects similarly depend on, but haven't yet fixed." With the latest development, Google has addressed a total of eight actively exploited Chrome zero-days since the start of the year. This includes CVE-2026-2441, CVE-2026-3909, CVE-2026-3910, CVE-2026-5281, CVE-2026-11645, CVE-2026-85046, and CVE-2026-87491. d2s85l.text: A public proof of concept has exposed a flaw in Telegram Desktop that could let attackers steal local files and take over accounts after a user clicks a crafted external link. Tracked as CVE-2026-107181, the vulnerability affects versions before 7.2.9 and carries a CVSS 4.0 severity rating of 8.6 (High). Researcher Beaksec published the technical write-up on October 3, 2026, and updated it on October 7. VulnCheck assigned the CVE that day. The reported attack reaches Telegram’s local session data, making account takeover possible when the victim has not enabled a local passcode. The weakness lies in how Telegram Desktop handles links opened outside the app. When Telegram is already running, another instance passes the link to it through a local communication channel, known as inter-process communication, or IPC. That channel failed to escape a character used to separate records. An attacker could place the character inside a crafted link and make Telegram read part of the link as another command. The CVE record classifies this as CWE-143, improper handling of record delimiters. PoC Released for Telegram Desktop Flaw According to ThreatWire’s research, the injected command could access an outdated internal helper designed for release publishing. The helper could read local files and send them to a chat without permission checks or user confirmation. The result is file theft through Telegram itself. Stolen session files could let an attacker reuse the victim’s logged-in account. Earlier reporting on Telegram account hijacking through voicemail shows another route to account loss, but that method is separate from this Desktop vulnerability. The researcher demonstrated the chain on Windows using Telegram Desktop 6.9.3 and reported that it remained present through 7.2.8. Although the CVE covers Telegram Desktop generally, the write-up does not demonstrate the attack on macOS or Linux. The link must be opened outside Telegram, such as from a browser. Links clicked inside Telegram follow a different processing path and are not affected. A browser may also ask for permission before launching the desktop app. The demonstrated chain depends on automatic group file downloads and settings that allow anyone to add the victim to a group. These conditions matter when judging the “one-click” claim. Previous EvilVideo coverage also highlighted download settings, although that issue affected Telegram for Android rather than Desktop. Telegram fixed the issue in commit db3405699f on September 16 and released version 7.2.9 on September 17. The reported changes remove the legacy helper, escape the record separator, and strengthen handling of mixed record types. The release notes mention only a rendering fix, not the security issue. No vendor security advisory is identified in the supplied reporting. The CVSS 3.1 score is 8.1, while CVSS 4.0 gives 8.6. Both ratings describe the same flaw. Users should update every Telegram Desktop installation to 7.2.9 or later. Until then, restrict group invitations, stop automatic downloads, and enable a local passcode. Treat unexpected browser prompts to open Telegram cautiously. As of October 9, the supplied reporting identifies no known exploitation or CISA KEV listing. A public PoC demonstrates feasibility, not confirmed attacks. The public write-up should not be mistaken for independent attack confirmation. Users who suspect exposure should end other active sessions and review chats for unexpected file uploads. Stops threats before impact with 21 min faster MTTR. oapp2e.text: Anthropic has introduced OSS Scanner, a free service that checks critical open-source repositories for security vulnerabilities and sends findings directly to project maintainers. The opt-in program uses the company’s strongest AI models to run repeated scans, giving developers a faster route to potential flaws without waiting for human review. According to Anthropic’s service overview, OSS Scanner builds on its work with Project Glasswing. The company says it had reviewed more than 6,000 vulnerability reports by October 2026 through its existing disclosure process. The new service offers a separate path for projects willing to assess AI-generated reports. Anthropic OSS Scanner According to the GitHub repository, the scanner first builds an enrolled project inside an isolated virtual machine with network access enabled. This stage installs dependencies and prepares the software for testing. Anthropic then removes Internet access before the security audit begins, allowing scanning agents to examine the project within a restricted environment. Reports arrive by email with steps to reproduce the suspected issue and a proposed patch where available. Anthropic says its pipeline includes agents that double-check bugs and examine their root causes. However, these checks are automated. A human does not review the findings before maintainers receive them. After the first scan, the service checks projects again for newly introduced vulnerabilities and issues missed earlier. Scan frequency depends on factors such as demand and project usage. This extends Anthropic’s wider push into security research, including earlier work in which Claude uncovered 22 Firefox vulnerabilities. Core maintainers apply through the official GitHub repository by opening a pull request that adds a directory under projects/<name>. Each submission needs a project.yaml configuration containing the repository address and a primary contact email. Anthropic manually checks that applicants are core maintainers before accepting a project. Eligibility focuses on established projects with broad use, exposure to remote attacks, and significant infrastructure security impact. A Dockerfile must explain how to install dependencies and build the software. Developers can keep it in their own repository or beside project.yaml in the enrollment repository. Everything needed for building and testing must be downloaded during setup because the later audit cannot access the Internet. An optional threat_model.md file helps guide the scan. Maintainers can describe where untrusted input enters, which components are outside scope, and how they rate severity. They can also explain preferred report formats and patch requirements, reducing the need for the scanner to guess project-specific security expectations. Before applying, developers can use tools/validate.py to check their configuration and tools/check <name> to test the build. The checking tool runs with network access, so Anthropic warns users to test only trusted projects or use a separate machine. Configuration email addresses are public, making a dedicated security alias useful. Maintainers can add an OpenPGP public key for encrypted reports, but encrypted messages go only to the primary contact and cannot include additional recipients. Anthropic does not impose a 90-day disclosure deadline on unvalidated findings. However, a report later confirmed through its human-reviewed program may enter that disclosure process. This safeguard matters amid concerns about AI-generated vulnerability reports wasting maintainers’ time. 1u9k9io.text: Let’s Encrypt will cut its default TLS certificate lifetime from 90 days to 64 days on February 10, 2027, giving website operators less time between renewals. The change applies to certificates issued or renewed from that date, while subscribers can still choose shorter certificate profiles offering 45 days or roughly six days. Let’s Encrypt Certificate Lifetime According to the October 7 announcement published by Let’s Encrypt, the nonprofit certificate authority confirmed the schedule. Existing certificates will remain valid until their normal expiry dates, and Let’s Encrypt will not revoke them as part of the transition. It expects the final 90-day certificate to expire on May 11, 2027. The shorter lifetime limits how long a certificate can remain trusted after a private key is stolen or a certificate is issued incorrectly. It also makes reliable renewal systems more important, especially for teams still using fixed schedules or manual steps. The move is part of the wider shift toward shorter public TLS certificate lifetimes. Cybersecurity News previously covered the CA/Browser Forum’s plan to reduce maximum validity to 47 days. Let’s Encrypt is moving faster, with its default profile set to 45 days on February 16, 2028, as outlined in its earlier certificate lifetime roadmap. Let’s Encrypt will start issuing 64-day certificates in its staging environment on October 14, 2026. Administrators can use this test service to check renewal behavior before the production change. Staging certificates are not trusted by browsers and should not replace certificates on live websites. For automated setups, the key feature is ACME Renewal Information, or ARI. ACME is the protocol used to request and renew certificates automatically. ARI lets Let’s Encrypt tell a supported client when to renew, helping it adjust to shorter lifetimes without relying on a fixed calendar. Administrators should check their client’s documentation to confirm ARI support. When ARI isn’t available, Let’s Encrypt recommends renewing at about two-thirds of the certificate’s lifetime. For a 64-day certificate, that means around day 43, rather than waiting until the old 60-day renewal point. The authority also recommends searching cron jobs, wrapper scripts, and runbooks for hardcoded values such as 83, 80, or 60. These numbers may reveal renewal rules designed around 90-day certificates. Updating those rules now also prepares systems for the 45-day default planned for 2028. Alongside certificate validity, Let’s Encrypt will reduce authorization reuse from 30 days to 10 days. This is the period during which an earlier domain control check can support another certificate request without repeating that check. The reuse period will fall to seven hours in 2028. Let’s Encrypt says this supports upcoming validation rules and removes the need for separate Certificate Authority Authorization rechecks on older validation data. Most subscribers will not need changes unless their ACME setup specifically depends on authorization reuse. Rate limits will not change because of the shorter lifetimes, according to Let’s Encrypt’s rate limit guidance. ACME endpoints and certificate issuance chains will also remain unchanged. Operators should test the full certificate workflow, including deployment and service reloads, rather than checking renewal alone. Teams managing many websites should also confirm that renewed certificates reach every server and that monitoring checks the certificate actually served to users after each reload. Alerts for failed renewals can help teams catch problems before expiry. The practical priority is dependable automation that keeps certificates current as renewal windows shrink. j5jng0.text: Microsoft is urging organizations to prepare their certificate systems for post-quantum authentication, warning that public key infrastructure (PKI), hardware security modules (HSMs), and security appliances need testing before deployment. Its October 8 guidance says the shift will affect applications, devices, certificate chains, and the processes that keep digital trust working. The message goes beyond protecting encrypted traffic. While many quantum security plans focus on attackers collecting data now to decrypt later, authentication depends on certificates and private keys being issued, stored, checked, renewed, and managed across different vendors. Changing the underlying algorithms can expose gaps across that entire chain. Microsoft Security Researchs noted that organizations often know where TLS protects communications but lack a complete view of certificate dependencies. Their report concerns infrastructure readiness, not a newly discovered malware campaign. Post-Quantum Authentication The main challenge is not simply finding a quantum-resistant algorithm. Businesses must establish whether their existing systems can use new certificates reliably. Older PKI deployments, embedded devices, operational technology, custom applications, and third-party services may contain fixed assumptions that only become visible during testing. Larger post-quantum certificates and certificate chains can affect connection setup, storage, transmission, and network inspection limits. Related work on Cloudflare’s post-quantum certificate authority shows why certificate size and connection speed matter as providers explore different designs for quantum-safe authentication. Those efforts do not remove the need to test enterprise systems individually. HSM providers and security appliance vendors therefore belong in the migration discussion from the start. Teams need to check whether hardware-backed systems support future certificate requirements and whether monitoring, inspection, and certificate-management tools can process the resulting traffic. Support in one application does not establish readiness across the full environment. Microsoft’s PQC TLS Pilot Microsoft launched its Post-Quantum Cryptography TLS Pilot Program on August 27, 2026. It allows approved certificate authorities in good standing with the Microsoft Trusted Root Program to test certificate roots and issuance using ML-DSA-87, a quantum-resistant digital signature algorithm. The focus is compatibility, performance, and day-to-day operations. The August release added seven pilot roots operated by ComSign, DigiCert, HARICA, IdenTrust Services, Sectigo, Shanghai Electronic Certification Authority, and SSL.com. Admissions continue through the end of 2026. Microsoft’s published authentication readiness guidance directs eligible providers to the Trusted Root Program portal for requirements and applications. These certificates are not publicly trusted. Microsoft limits their use to closed environments, custom applications, and enterprise testbeds, explicitly excluding production trust and public-facing websites. Elsewhere, Let’s Encrypt’s certificate roadmap explores Merkle Tree Certificates for public-web authentication, highlighting that separate efforts are addressing different parts of the transition. On supported, correctly configured Windows 11 systems, pilot testing begins with the July 28, 2026 updates. Microsoft names KB5101681, OS Build 28000.2608, for 26H1, and KB5101684, OS Builds 26200.8973 and 26100.8973, for 25H2. ML-DSA certificates can also work with Secure Channel, or Schannel, in supported scenarios. Administrators must confirm platform requirements before testing. Software and hardware readiness should be checked separately. Earlier coverage of Google’s quantum-safe digital signatures described software-based Cloud KMS support with hardware-backed support planned separately. Microsoft similarly urges organizations to ask certificate providers, HSM vendors, software suppliers, and platform vendors about their roadmaps and testing capabilities rather than assume universal support. Security teams should inventory certificate-dependent systems, map public and private trust relationships, and identify equipment with long upgrade cycles. Non-production tests should cover compatibility, performance, and operational workflows. Developments such as OpenSSL’s post-quantum performance improvements offer useful testing context, but preview software and Microsoft’s pilot certificates should not be treated as production-ready replacements. That work should include the full certificate lifecycle, not just a successful connection. Issuance, distribution, validation, renewal, and management all depend on linked systems. Testing those steps together helps teams find process gaps that a standalone algorithm test could miss before they reach live business services. Microsoft recommends a multi-year program with named owners, clear dependencies, and modernization priorities based on test results. Organizations can ask their certificate provider whether it participates in the pilot and offers suitable testing. The practical goal is to uncover failures before quantum-resistant authentication becomes a large-scale deployment requirement. 6tjopr.text: VirusTotal has added daily scanning of the public IPv4 space, giving security teams a new way to find command-and-control (C2) servers and track malware infrastructure. Announced on October 8, 2026, the update records exposed services, port activity, banners, and server fingerprints alongside existing threat intelligence. The change helps researchers look beyond an IP address’s detection score. Earlier reports showed hosting details, passive DNS records, and files that contacted an address. The new data shows what a server exposes now, helping analysts find related hosts that have no malware detections. A new Ports tab lists open, closed, and recently closed ports, together with service names, software versions, and timestamps. Records also include SSH host keys, RDP fingerprints, HTTP headers, and operating system details inferred from service responses. VirusTotal keeps records when ports stop responding. Researchers can therefore check when a suspected C2 service was last seen online and compare that date with changes elsewhere in a campaign. This history adds context that a current detection score cannot provide. VirusTotal Adds Daily Internet Scanning The official announcement describes searches through the web interface and API. Queries such as entity:ip open_port:22 find exposed SSH services. Bracket syntax ties conditions to specific ports, preventing a product on one port from being incorrectly matched with a version on another. These searches build on the methods covered in Cybersecuritynews.com’s VirusTotal threat research guide. One investigation started with 91.219.237[.]110, an address listed in APT28 and Havoc collections. Its SSH fingerprint led researchers to 185.146.232[.]3, which had no detections, collections, or communicating files. Both hosts shared an OpenSSH build, nginx configuration, and an unusual certificate name, b4ck.my. Searching that certificate name uncovered a third address, 96.9.125[.]59. Port timestamps suggested one server was being retired around the time another appeared. However, VirusTotal warned that older malware links do not establish current ownership or APT28 attribution because IP addresses can change hands. Fingerprint matches also need careful checks. Some SSH keys appeared across more than 1,400 cloud addresses because server templates reused them. An open port alone is similarly weak evidence. Searching Cobalt Strike’s default team server port returned over 1.5 million addresses, including hosts answering on many ports. Another example exposed a NOX Stealer login panel at 5.175.221[.]206 on port 8443. The host also exposed SMB and RDP, with scan data identifying Windows Server 2022, nginx 1.24.0, and PHP 8.3.33. Combining those traits reduced a search from 4.5 million hosts to ten candidates, not ten confirmed malicious servers. When the panel changed its name to BOMBAY Stealer, browser analysis captured the new title while the exposed services stayed unchanged. Researchers also searched FTP banners containing “conhost,” finding five addresses tied to command-delivery patterns discussed in E4del and PINHOLE research. Port data is available through API records and history endpoints, but not yet through IP Livehunt rules. Saved searches run on a schedule offer a workaround. fow618.text: Alleged internal chats from Silent Ransom Group suggest the criminals collected $206.95 million from 27 firms in roughly six months without encrypting victims’ files. The reported earnings point to the power of data extortion, where attackers steal sensitive records and demand payment to keep them private. However, the payment figures remain unverified, and the group denies breaching its systems or leaking its chats. DataBreaches reported the alleged leak on October 7. The material contains 5,692 messages covering August 27, 2025, through September 29, 2026. Discussions reportedly include victim negotiations, payments, access methods, and members’ spending. An October 8 update said Silent Ransom Group had agreed to an interview but disputed the leak’s origin. Silent Ransomware Extorted Over $200,000,000 The chats mark completed deals as “GOLD.” Adding those entries produces the $206.95 million total. Crystal Intelligence dates the 27 claimed payments between April 3 and September 24, 2026, placing the reported earnings within a period of less than six months. These entries reflect the criminals’ own records, not audited financial results. According to DataBreaches, the median alleged payment was $6 million, while individual amounts ranged from $100,000 to $30 million. White & Case was listed against the largest amount. Nine named firms disclosed breaches relevant to the period. However, those disclosures do not confirm who attacked them or whether they paid the sums shown. Crystal Intelligence’s blockchain analysis found transactions matching the timing of several chat entries. One upstream collection wallet received about 344 bitcoin, valued at roughly $27 million, over six weeks. Researchers could not connect individual victim payments to that wallet. Hence, the evidence supports substantial money movement rather than proving the headline total. Operators trick employees into granting access, steal documents, and threaten to publish them. Law firms have been a major focus because they hold private client information. CybersecurityNews previously covered the group’s IT support impersonation attacks against law firms. Attackers call employees, pose as internal support staff, and persuade them to grant remote access. Legitimate software helps the activity blend into routine work, reducing reliance on malware that security tools might otherwise detect. Related reporting on Luna Moth’s fake helpdesk domains describes websites designed to resemble company support services. Once they gain access, tools such as WinSCP and Rclone can transfer stolen files. The pressure comes from the possible disclosure of confidential records, not a sudden loss of access to business systems. Crystal found instructions to use fresh wallets, keep victim funds separate, and avoid combining payouts. Operators sometimes broke those rules, linking transactions investigators could trace. Smaller payments also reached regulated exchanges, creating potential leads through customer identity records. The analysis describes cash conversion through instant exchangers, couriers, and a Bitcoin-to-Zelle service. For defenders, the attack chain makes identity checks essential. Employees should verify support requests through known internal channels before granting access. Organizations should restrict remote access, deploy phishing-resistant authentication, and train staff to recognize phone-based deception. Working systems don’t prove sensitive files stay safe. 1w6ljoy.text: A malicious Android PDF reader distributed through Google Play has recorded more than 10,000 installs while serving as an installer for the Anatsa banking trojan. The finding shows how a routine document tool can become a route for malware that puts banking passwords and financial accounts at risk. The installation figure describes the reach of the reader app, not a confirmed count of successful banking infections or stolen accounts. The available alert also does not identify affected banks, victim countries, financial losses, or whether Google has since removed this particular listing, wile those details remain unconfirmed. Researchers from Zscaler ThreatLabz identified the malicious installer and shared its indicators in an October 8 alert on X. They described the application as an Android PDF reader with over 10,000 installs and published separate file hashes for the installer and the Anatsa payload, alongside their command-and-control addresses. The discovery follows earlier cases involving similar disguises. In April, a fake document reader campaign used a different package to distribute Anatsa before Google removed that app. That earlier removal should not be confused with the status of the newly reported reader, which the current alert does not establish. Malicious PDF Reader With 10,000+ Installs Anatsa, also known as TeaBot, uses a dropper model: the app installed first acts as a delivery tool for a separate malicious component. This separation helps explain why a download that appears useful can later expose a phone to banking malware. The latest alert identifies both stages but does not provide a full execution trace. In its technical analysis of Anatsa, ThreatLabz documented earlier campaigns that downloaded additional code and presented the final payload as an app update. Some samples checked the device environment before proceeding, helping the malware avoid test systems used by researchers. These are documented family techniques, not confirmed findings for every new sample. ThreatLabz also documented malformed APK archive headers that made older payloads harder to inspect, along with encrypted code loaded at runtime. APK files are Android installation packages; hiding their contents can disrupt tools that inspect files without running them. The new alert does not confirm whether these samples use those methods. The broader use of Google Play stealth loaders shows why unexpected update requests deserve attention even when the original app came from an official store. A request to install an extra component outside the normal update process can move the user from a harmless-looking utility to the banking payload. ThreatLabz has uncovered another new Anatsa installer that is distributed via the Google Play Store. The application is disguised as an Android PDF reader that currently has over 10,000 installs. The IOCs for this campaign are listed below: Google Play Store URL… pic.twitter.com/duQA0myTAi — Zscaler ThreatLabz (@Threatlabz) October 8, 2026 For this campaign, ThreatLabz listed one installer-related command-and-control URL and two payload command-and-control endpoints. Keeping those roles separate matters during an investigation: the installer and the banking trojan are different files, and each has its own published MD5 hash. The alert does not explain the exact contents returned by the installer URL. Why Banking Accounts Are at Risk Earlier ThreatLabz research found that Anatsa requested SMS and accessibility permissions, contacted its control server, and checked for targeted financial apps. The server then supplied fake login pages matching apps on the phone. Credentials entered into those pages were sent to the attackers rather than the bank. A previous Anatsa document reader outbreak reached more than 100,000 downloads and used fake banking screens to capture account details. That history explains the concern around this new reader, but its target list and permission behavior still require sample-specific verification rather than assumptions based on older campaigns. What Android Users Should Do Users who installed the identified reader should remove it, review granted permissions, and scan their phones with a trusted security tool. Keep Google Play Protect enabled and question unexpected requests for SMS or accessibility access. If banking activity looks suspicious, contact the bank promptly and change account passwords from a trusted device. For security teams, the package name can support app inventory checks, while file hashes help match samples against the reported installer and payload. Network logs can be searched for the listed domain and IP endpoints. Matches should be reviewed in context to establish which device communicated, when contact occurred, and whether malware executed. 130wolt.text: Open-source AI platform Artex is being used prolifically by cybercriminals and nation-states to breach government agencies and dozens of critical sectors worldwide, according to a new FBI advisory. The FBI released a flash alert on Friday about the tool, which has caused alarm among cybersecurity experts for its ability to take any large language model and turn it into a powerful hacking tool that can “automate multiple phases of cyber intrusions at machine speed, from reconnaissance through data exfiltration.” “Artex significantly reduces the time required to chain attack techniques, with some intrusions progressing from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours,” the FBI said. “The framework enables threat actors with minimal technical expertise to conduct complex, multi-target operations simultaneously, fundamentally accelerating attack velocity and expanding operational scale.” The tool was released in August on GitHub by an account known as "Autumn-27.” The developer of the framework — identified as Chinese cybersecurity engineer Li Puhua — released a statement on GitHub on October 8 saying the tool was abused by malicious actors. The developer denied any responsibility for crimes committed with it and eventually removed the GitHub repository. The FBI said on Friday that despite the removal, the framework “continues to proliferate through community forks, localized variations, archived copies, and a commercial version … ensuring continued availability to threat actors.” The advisory cites recent research from cybersecurity firm Censys showing over 1,600 publicly exposed Artex console instances, with total deployments likely significantly higher when including systems behind firewalls or in private networks. The penetration testing platform can translate high-level tactical goals described in words into actionable machine commands executed by AI agents, requiring minimal human interaction beyond the initial objectives. Artex can integrate any AI model, including frontier models Anthropic Claude and OpenAI GPT as well as open-source or Chinese-origin models like DeepSeek, GLM, Grok and Kimi. “Analysis of attacker-controlled Artex instances shows Chinese models are most prevalent, with DeepSeek Flash family models dominating usage due to their balance of capabilities, relatively low cost, and lack of observable guardrails when framed for penetration testing,” the FBI explained. The tool has been used to conduct reconnaissance and data exfiltration attacks targeting financial services, government, technology, defense, semiconductor, energy, healthcare, manufacturing, telecommunications and legal industries. It was recently implicated in multiple attacks on South Korean and Japanese financial institutions, causing national scandals in both countries. Microsoft said Artex was used by Chinese state-backed actors in a recent supply chain attack on IT management software company ConnectWise. Amazon joined the fray on Friday, releasing its own study finding “disparate Chinese-nexus threat groups” using Artex for “a large-scale theft of credentials to access AI models, organized as a self-sustaining operation in which stolen keys paid for the LLM inference powering further credential hunting.” “Another campaign targeted cryptocurrency exchanges for know-your-customer (KYC) verification bypass using real-time deepfake injection,” Amazon CISO CJ Moses said. Moses argued their investigation showed that frameworks like Artex “have progressed from experimental use to sustained, multi-objective offensive operations that run with minimal human intervention.” They warned that Artex is automating time-consuming phases of exploitation and is allowing smaller threat groups to run concurrent intrusion campaigns at a scale they previously could not. Agents deployed by Artex have shown an ability to “map trust relationships between organizations” and compromise weak third-party vendors. Artex is adept at identifying and exploiting systems that have less security attention than others, including “partner and supplier portals, mobile backends, employee applications, sales-support systems, legacy services, third-party integrations, and applications created across different business units,” the FBI explained. The tool generates a high-volume of attempts that will set off defense sensors but works at a speed that makes it difficult for defenders to keep up. 5f8bam.text: The New York City Council has approved a bill barring retailers and other businesses from using surveillance pricing to harness customers’ personal data as a means of charging different people variable amounts for the same product. The metropolis is the second city in the country to pass legislation banning surveillance pricing, following Seattle, where a similar ban was signed into law last month. The New York City Council voted 44-5 on Thursday in favor of the bill and Mayor Zohran Mamdani celebrated its passage, telling the media “when corporations use your personal data to decide what you pay, you only stand to lose.” The bill allows the city’s Department of Consumer and Worker Protection to fine companies deploying surveillance pricing up to $1,000 for each violation, but carves out “bona fide discounts and rewards that are legitimate and transparent, from buy-one-get-one-free deals and loyalty programs to discounts for veterans and students,” according to a council press release. The bill is a “big deal for a few reasons,” according to Grace Gedye, a Consumer Reports policy analyst who worked on the effort to push it through. “Once this bill becomes law and goes into effect, it will mean eight million fewer people will have to guess about whether their search history, what they are hovering over online, and more, is shaping the price they see,” Gedye said via email. “It also means a lot of businesses may need to change their pricing practices — and if they already have to do it for New York City, they may decide to do it for the rest of the country at the same time.” Gedye noted that the New York state legislature passed a similar surveillance pricing law in June, but said the bill has been sitting unsigned on Gov. Kathy Hochul’s desk for several months. Advocates worry that even if Hochul signs the state legislation, she could use an unusual New York statute allowing governors to unilaterally amend passed bills to weaken its language. New Jersey, Connecticut and Maryland already have similar bans on the books and many more state legislators nationwide are expected to introduce bills when new sessions begin early next year, said George Slover, senior counsel for competition policy at the Center for Democracy and Technology. ‘Viscerally offensive’ “There is a lot of interest around the country in this issue,” Slover said in an interview. “It's viscerally offensive to consumers to think about the fact that they are being basically sized up for their willingness to pay more and eliminate the advantage that they've had all these years, where … the consumer is essentially anonymous when the price is set.” With the price of food and other consumer goods increasing and data brokers selling businesses detailed consumer profiles — including about spending habits and demographics — there is widespread suspicion that different consumers are being charged varying amounts based on algorithms. Grocery stores, ride sharing companies and airlines are thought to be widely using surveillance pricing, but public evidence is limited. Lawmakers and regulators are acting anyway. In October, the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) ordered nine food delivery, airline, ride-sharing and retail companies to answer extensive questions about how they exploit personal data to set higher prices for some consumers and less compensation for select employees. Companies receiving the orders include major airlines, Uber, DoorDash, Walmart and Target. FTC officials have said they plan to study the “opaque methodology” used to set prices in an era when powerful new technologies, data brokers and algorithms can be easily tapped into to reveal granular information about specific shoppers. In 2022, Target paid $5 million to settle a lawsuit brought by several California district attorneys who charged the tech giant showed customers’ standing in the parking lot lower prices than those in store. Last year, a San Francisco news outlet revealed that by changing a web browser’s location, its reporter found customers in the Midwest and Phoenix were charged less than customers in San Francisco for the same New York City hotel rooms. Advocates have long charged that the Kroger grocery store chain uses surveillance pricing though the company has steadfastly denied the charges. However, the nonprofit Consumer Reports has revealed Kroger deploys advanced technology to track shoppers' purchases and behaviors, selling the data to third-party companies for targeted advertising. Kroger also has confirmed that it uses digital price tags to quickly tweak pricing though it has said changes are not made based on personal data. She was previously a cybersecurity reporter at CyberScoop. Earlier in her career Suzanne covered the Boston Police Department for the Boston Globe and two presidential campaign cycles for Newsweek. She lives in Washington with her husband and three children.

ox1ci1.text: The city of Osaka notified the public that a data breach involving a third-party technology provider exposed more than 1 million email addresses tied to an online administrative services platform. According to a statement published by the government of Japan’s third-largest city, hackers accessed the Arara email distribution service used by TKC Corporation, the company contracted to maintain the administrative services platform. Anyone who received an email from the system run by the city between July 2026 and October 31 had their email address leaked, according to the city. They warned the city’s 2.8 million residents to be wary of suspicious emails purporting to come from the city — urging everyone not to open any URLs or attachments. The city breach came days after the regional government of the Osaka Prefecture announced its own data breach involving the information of food support program participants. The attack on Arara has had a cascading effect on dozens of large businesses and governments in Japan. The company said a November 2 cyberattack exposed 77 million email addresses from nearly 400 customers, including TKC, gaming giant Sega and others. Arara noted that hackers used their email distribution service to send millions of malicious emails pretending to be credit card companies and financial institutions. ‘Let us mobilize’ Japan has been rocked by months of cyberattacks on critical companies and institutions — from Japan Airlines to Sony Network Communications and gaming company Capcom. Last week, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi held a cabinet meeting on cybersecurity and announced a package of emergency measures aimed at increasing the use of AI for cyber defense, more robust information gathering, offensive cyberattacks and increased support for data breach victims. About $62 million in emergency funds were dedicated to the effort and companies were urged to report cyberattacks more quickly to government agencies. “Even at this very moment, incidents of unauthorized access and information leaks continue to occur, significantly affecting people's daily lives and business activities,” she said. “Let us mobilize the full resources of the government to strengthen Japan's overall capabilities to respond to cyberattacks.” Japan's national Computer Security Incident Response Team published a study three weeks ago that said it found evidence attackers are using AI to scan for known vulnerabilities before carrying out attacks in the country. Mihoko Matsubara, the chief cybersecurity strategist at Japanese telecom giant NTT, told Recorded Future News that recent data showed cyberattacks on Japanese systems began to grow in July and skyrocketed through October. October saw 58% of all reported incidents this year in Japan, she said. About 380 million pieces of personal data have been stolen so far this year. A large amount of Japanese personal information is already being traded on the dark web, and some of the data has been used for fraudulent securities transactions, Matsubara said, warning that determined actors with financial resources could compile a comprehensive database of Japanese citizens' socioeconomic activities and personal preferences. Matsubara, who previously worked for Japan’s Ministry of Defense and other government cybersecurity committees, noted that the recent surge in breaches came after new cybersecurity legislation came into effect that allows the government to take more robust action in the event of a significant cyberattack. “Many countries would be keen to learn how quickly Japan would respond to which kinds of cyberattacks, and with what level of intensity,” she said. Matsubara added that the recent breaches appear to involve AI-tools like Claude and Artex, which help cybercriminals uncover and exploit bugs. But she argued that not every breach in this wave can be attributed to AI. The most important aspect of the government initiatives announced last week is the acknowledgement that cybersecurity “cannot be left entirely to individual organizations.” “Government assistance, in the form of security assessments and incident response or recovery support, can make a difference when push comes to shove,” she said. “However, the funding needs to be the beginning of a consistent longer-term effort, and cannot be seen as a one-time quick fix to the current wave of attacks.” No previous articleNo new articlesJonathan Greigis a Breaking News Reporter at Recorded Future News. 1m7lwmk.text: Cryptocurrency hardware wallet maker Trezor has confirmed that three Safe 5 devices sold by Southeast Asian reseller CryptoBilis contained malicious hardware implants designed to steal wallet recovery phrases and send them to attackers over cellular networks. The findings follow an investigation into a suspected hardware implant first reported in October, when a customer discovered an unauthorized circuit board inside a Trezor Safe 5 purchased from Indonesian reseller CryptoBilis. At the time, Trezor had not received the device for examination and could not confirm the implant's capabilities. In a new investigation update, the company says it has now examined the original device in its laboratory and identified two additional compromised wallets using photographs submitted by their owners. All three compromised devices were purchased from CryptoBilis between August 20 and September 23, 2026. Trezor says 48 CryptoBilis customers have contacted the company following its October warning, with devices being examined in its laboratory or through photographs of their internal components. The company has also inspected devices from other resellers in the region and found no evidence of tampering. So far, the confirmed implants have been limited to Safe 5 devices sold through CryptoBilis, and no affected customers have reported losing funds. Firmware update blocks hardware implants Trezor says its engineers analyzed the implant's firmware and confirmed that the malicious hardware can capture sensitive information displayed or entered on the wallet's screen. The implant consists of an additional circuit board installed between the Safe 5's main board and display, allowing it to monitor screen activity without modifying the device's legitimate firmware or Secure Element. When wallet recovery words appear on the screen, either during the creation of a new wallet backup or while restoring an existing wallet, the implant collects them. It can also capture passphrases displayed on the screen, encrypt the stolen information, and transmit it over a mobile network to an attacker-controlled server. If a connection is unavailable, the implant holds on to the captured data and repeatedly attempts to transmit it until successful. These reported implants follow confirmed hardware implants previously discovered in Ledger devices sold through CryptoBilis, which have been linked to cryptocurrency thefts. On November 11, Trezor released firmware version 2.13.1, which includes protections that prevent the implants from capturing information. "Our latest firmware update 2.13.1, released on November 11th, includes a protection that stops the implants we’ve found from capturing anything on devices that run it, making the current batch of implants useless," Trezor said. However, the company warns that the update cannot protect wallet recovery phrases that may have already been captured before it was installed. While no Trezor customers have reported stolen funs, those who purchased Trezor devices from CryptoBilis are still advised to transfer their cryptocurrency to a newly created wallet using a new recovery phrase. Trezor Safe 5 genuine hardware compared with implanted device Source: Trezor Trezor cuts reseller network by 80% Due to these supply-chain attacks, Trezor has reduced its global reseller network by approximately 80%, significantly reducing the number of third-party resellers of its hardware wallets. The company previously announced plans to reduce its reseller network in October, following reports of compromised Ledger wallets sold through CryptoBilis. This was before Trezor had learned of implants in its devices as well. Trezor says the removed resellers were trustworthy and of no threat, but did not meet the stricter supply-chain security requirements being introduced. Remaining partners must follow tighter controls governing how devices are sourced, stored, and accessed. The company is offering replacement devices to anyone who purchased a Trezor wallet from CryptoBilis since March 2026, including customers whose devices have not been confirmed as compromised. At this time, the company says it has found no evidence of device implants from other resellers and has received no reports of funds being stolen through the compromised Safe 5 wallets.
